subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASED PENSIONS FOR SUPERANNUATED CIVIL SERVANTS, ARMED FORCES PERSONNEL AND MOUNTED POLICE

speechtext:
Hon.	Donald	M.	Fleming (Minister	ofFinance): I should like to make a statement, Mr. Speaker, relating to the provision which the government intends to recommend to parliament at the present session to increase pensions, based	on	length of service,	offormer	members	of	the civil service,	thearmed	forces,	and	the Royal Canadian
Mounted Police, in those cases where the recipient has been retired for a number of years. The proposed provision will also extend to the widows and children of former members of the three groups on a similar basis.
In the course of long personal study of this subject, I have found it one of the most complex problems which I have faced in this portfolio. It would have been the wish of the government to bring this proposal before parliament at an earlier date had the problem admitted of an easier or simpler solution.
Apart from the relatively minor increase which was made in the pensions of certain former members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in 1925, the measure now proposed is unprecedented in Canada in federal legislation dealing with long-service pensions. Prior to 1945 the pensions of the
three groups I have mentioned were such that there was no strong demand for an increase. Since 1946, however, a combination of the rise in the cost of living and in the general salary levels of the three groups in the public service has led to increasing representations not only by retired members of the three groups but by members of the house and the various civil service organizations.
The representations affect pensions related to length of service, and accordingly the present proposal does not affect pensions payable under the Government Employees Compensation Act, the Pension Act, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act in respect only of disability or death arising from service, nor pensions payable under part IV of the last named act.
There are, in round figures, 23,000 former civil servants or their widows in receipt of pension. Of these 10,000 are over 70 years of age and 6,700 are between the ages of 65 and 70. The government decided, however, that old age pensions and old age assistance should not be taken into account in determining the proposed increases in pensions based on length of service.
A survey which has been recently conducted shows that in most cases the small pensions are attributable to short service. While at times in the past a pension could be paid for less than five years' service, now under the Public Service Superannuation Act the cases where a pension can be paid for such short service have almost disappeared, and the normal pension is payable on retirement for age or disability after a minimum of five years of service, and a widow's pension is payable if her husband had at least five years of service. Thus a minimum pension of 10 per cent of average salary is payable in the case of a civil servant himself or 5 per cent in the case of his widow.
The survey has also demonstrated that, as a result of the general increases in salaries in recent years, persons retiring in this period can receive higher pensions after shorter service than those who retired from the same positions in earlier years with longer service. This situation has naturally caused dissatisfaction.
It does not seem to the government to be fair to the employee with long service to supplement only the very low pensions.

Public Service-Pension Increase Generally speaking this would tend to favour those who have given a relatively brief portion of their working lives to the service of the federal government, or those employees who rendered longer service in quite junior positions.
It is equally clear that a flat percentage increase in all pensions would be inequitable. It would favour those now enjoying the larger pensions, particularly those who retired recently. Moreover, the pensioners who retired ten years ago have a higher claim for an increase in their pensions than those who have been retired more recently with pensions more closely related to the present higher scale of salaries.
On the other hand, if the basis of increase were a flat percentage confined simply to all pensions commencing prior to a determined date, a pensioner retiring immediately prior to that date would have an unjustified advantage over a person retiring immediately thereafter with the same service to his credit.
There is an additional complication to be considered even for those retiring at the same time, because of the fact that there are six different benefit formulae to be considered when determining what increase should be made in the pensions of the three groups under review, namely former civil servants, members of the armed forces and members of the R.C.M.P. Depending upon the time at which the individual affected qualified under the relevant pension statute, he will have received a pension of 2 per cent of a certain salary or average salary over a certain period for each year of service up to 35. This period on which the average salary is based ranges from the most favourable extreme of the final salary in the case of long-time members of the armed forces and the R.C.M.P. to the average salary over the last ten-year period of employment in the case of civil servants. In between these extremes there are four other formulae using the salary for the last year and the average salary over the last three, five and six years of service respectively. The fact that pensions are payable to members of the armed forces and the R.C.M.P. immediately on retirement at an age which may be earlier than the civil service immediate pension age of 60 makes the usual military or R.C.M.P. pension even more valuable than the usual civil service pension.
In the studies which have been made it has been recognized that those whose salary for pension purposes is based on the shorter period of time will retire on pensions more closely related to the level of salaries at the time of retirement than do the ten-year average cases, and so will have gained a greater pension benefit from general salary increases in their last years of employment.

The government has come to the conclusion that the method of adjustment chosen should take account of these factors, otherwise the disparity in pension as among the various groups would become even greater. For this purpose more than one series of adjustment factors has been worked out in relation to the change which has taken place during the period on which the average salary in question is based. This method has the effect of bringing closer together pensions for the same period of service and salary under the different formulae.
After careful study of all the complicated factors involved, the government proposes an increase of a maximum of 32 per cent of the first $2,000 of the pension of those pensioners who retired in 1945 and earlier years. The percentage of increase will be lower for those retiring since 1945. The effect of this graduation in the increase will confine benefit as follows: To those who retired prior to 1953, on the ten-year average formula; to those who retired prior to 1952, on the six-year average formula; to those who retired prior to 1951, on the five-year average formula; to those who retired prior to 1950, on the three-year average formula; to those who retired prior to 1949, on the final year formula; to those who retired prior to 1948, under the final salary formula. This difference in the cut-off dates arises from the fact that those whose pension formula is based on the shorter average salary period have already gained a benefit from that formula in the form of a higher pension as the result of the introduction in the years just before their retirement of general salary increases which helped to a much lesser extent those subject to the longer average salary period.
It is proposed that the increase in the pension shall be confined to pensions not exceeding $3,000 per annum, and that the total of the increase and the pension combined shall not exceed $3,000.
In the case of widows and children the percentage of increase will be that appropriate to the year of the husband's retirement or death while in the service, whichever is applicable, and will be calculated on the first $1,000 of pension for a widow, with corresponding amounts for the children. The increase will be limited, in the case of a widow, to pensions not exceeding $1,500; and in the case of her child to pensions not exceeding $300. In the case of an orphan child the increase will apply on pensions not exceeding $600. In each of these cases the pension and increase combined will not exceed these respective amounts.
It is estimated that the increases will apply to some 15,000 pensioners, including 12,000

former civil servants, 2,500 former members of the armed forces and 600 former members of the R.C.M.P. These figures include the widows of deceased pensioners. The estimated cost of the increase is approximately $3,300,000, for a full year at present.
The government proposes that the increases take effect from July 1. In view of the advanced stage of the present session the government proposes to insert a special item in the further supplementary estimates which will be introduced in parliament at the present session to provide for the payment during the present fiscal year. Further details will be available at that time. It is the government's intention at the next session to introduce legislation to provide continuing authority for these increases. It is expected that the retroactive payments will be available to recipients in the autumn. The precise date will naturally depend on the course and duration of the present session.
In conclusion I should like to express my gratitude to the advisory committee of the Public Service Superannuation Act for the very helpful advice I have received from time to time from that group, which is composed of equal representation from the official and staff sides of the public service.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR JOINT LOANS TO TOURIST RESORT OPERATORS

speakeroldname: Mr. G. H. Aiken (Parry Sound-Muskoka) moved:
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR JOINT LOANS TO TOURIST RESORT OPERATORS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of introducing legislation to authorize the making of loans, jointly with an approved lending institu-
2760	HOUSE OF
Loans to Tourist Resort Operators tion, to tourist resort operators for the purpose of constructing or making capital improvements to tourist accommodation.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the subject of this resolution is of considerable urgency and interest both to the people of this country and to hon. members of the house. I feel that it has received insufficient attention from a large section of the population and, moreover, I think the subject is one which has not been recently discussed in parliament.
Before proceeding to deal with the financial aspect of the resolution, I should like to place the tourist industry in its proper perspective with regard to the national income. As a direct source of foreign money the tourist industry in Canada ranks third after newsprint and wheat. In 1957 we received in Canada no less than $362 million in tourist funds from all sources in connection with the tourist industry. In 1957 the tourist resort industry came second among Canada's industries in terms of receipt of United States dollars. In that year $328 million came to Canada from the United States in connection with the tourist business. The tourist business comes third in receipt of foreign dollars from all sources and second in receipt of United States dollars.
In the third place, the tourist industry is a major source of employment in this country. The indirect sources of employment are much greater than the direct. For that reason we sometimes do not consider that the published figures are correct. If we consider merely those dollars that come into the country and if we consider merely those dollars received by the tourist industry itself we do not get a complete picture, because we must consider all the money that is spent in Canada by tourists in places that are not tourist locations. For instance, we must consider the merchandise they purchase, the money they spend in restaurants and stores and things of that nature to get a complete understanding of the situation.
The tourist economy is important for another reason. It does not require any outlay by the government or any public services. The product involved in the tourist industry, as it were, is the beauty of Canada's scenery and her rich resources. The only thing the government has had to do thus far has been to advertise, and that has been very well done by various government agencies. The tourist industry does not deplete our natural resources. Those who come to visit Canada, for the most part, come to look at our scenery. They take away with them the memory of a holiday spent in beautiful surroundings, but they


take nothing more of a physical nature except those goods they have purchased.
Another feature of this industry is that we do not have to transport any particular product to market. We do not have to do what must be done in connection with wheat and many other products which have to be shipped to some other country. In the case of the tourist industry the people come here to buy the product.
And finally, the tourist industry is something we in Canada have taken for granted for some time, and therefore through neglect we are beginning to lose the position we held in this industry. As to the future of travel, we must bear in mind that travel has developed from a luxury on the North American continent to a way of life. There has been a general increase in wages and a shorter work week, and employees are now granted longer paid holidays. All these things have combined to give the average individual on this continent more time in which to travel and see the world. Properly managed and planned, the tourist industry could and should become Canada's major industry.
I wish to say a few words by way of comparison between Canada's tourist industry and that of the United Kingdom. The tourist industry in the United Kingdom is without question the most important industry of that country. Let us look at Canada for a moment in its relationship to other countries in terms of this industry. Not very long ago Canada used to be the No. 1 country for United States travellers.
We do not need to extol the beauties of our native country. I will have a few words to say about the particular area in which I am interested, and I am sure other members will also wish to mention those in which they are interested. Every province and territory in Canada has many places which can compare with those anywhere else in the world, but in spite of this we are losing business while others are increasing theirs.
To look at some of the figures, Mr. Speaker, in 1948 about 45 per pent of the United States tourist dollar came to Canada. That was only 10 years ago. In 1951 it was down to 35 per cent. In 1952 we commenced to have a trade deficit with the United States in travel account. In dollars Canadians spent $37 million more in the United States in 1952 than United States tourists spent in Canada. In 1956 our percentage of the United States tourist dollar was down to about 25 per cent and our trade deficit in travel was $82 million.
I should like to point out the significance of these figures. We had in 1956 a trade

deficit on travel of approximately $161 million on a world-wide basis. The United States has a population ten times ours, yet Canadians spent many millions of dollars more in the United States than the people of that country spent in Canada. Our 17 million people spent more than they spent in Canada with their population of approximately 170 million.
On the basis of world-wide travel the situation is the same. From 1926 until 1950 we had a world travel credit balance, but since 1951 we have had a travel deficit with all countries of the world. I am pleased to see from the figures that there was a little improvement last year. Our deficit with the United States dropped from $82 million to $75 million. However, taking the whole picture the position remained the same, with a deficit of $161 million with all countries.
I should like to quote for a minute from a publication entitled, "Travel Between Canada and the United States", issued in January, 1958, which gives preliminary figures for 1957. It says:
Expenditures in Canada by travellers from the United States and other countries set a new record in 1957. First estimates indicate that visitors from other countries spent approximately $362 million while travelling in Canada, an increase of $25 million or approximately 7 per cent higher than the previous year. Receipts from residents of the United States advanced some $19 million, due to higher average expenditures per visit for most classifications in addition to an increase in the number of crossings. The aggregate number of visits advanced some 953,000 when compared with 1956. The estimated figure of $328 million spent in Canada by residents of the United States is an all-time record, although residents of countries other than the United States also increased their expenditures on travel in Canada during 1957. Receipts from residents of overseas countries reached a new record of $34 million, an increase of $6 million over the previous record established in 1956.
This indicates that we have had more visitors to Canada during the past year than in previous years. But I quote again from the same document:
The gain in foreign travel expenditures in Canada was accompanied by a more moderate increase in Canadian travel to other countries, particularly to the United States. Canadians spent an estimated $23 million on travel in other countries during the past year, an increase of $25 million over 1956 or approximately 5 per cent. The increase of travel expenditures in the United States amounted to $12 million or some 3 per cent, whereas expenditures on travel to overseas countries advanced some 12 per cent or about $13 million as compared with the previous year.
While our receipts from travel expenditures are increasing, as they naturally will, our expenditures in other countries have also increased. There has been a decrease in the past in certain classifications of travel to this country. As I previously noted, we had 45
28, 1958
Loans to Tourist Resort Operators per cent of the United States tourist dollar in 1948 and now we have less than 25 per cent.
For a moment I should like to look into what I feel are the reasons for this decline. We are losing business from United States tourists to the European market. There seems to be an increase in the number of people who travel overseas from the United States. We are also losing very extensively to the United States home market. Under the small business administration in the United States hotel or resort owners can borrow up to $250,000 for renovating or refurnishing their resorts, the loan being repayable over a period of 10 years at an interest rate of 5 or 6 per cent. By making funds available to the United States home market people there are enabled to improve their accommodation and offer more attractions for their own tourists.
There are also more Canadians going to the United States rather than travelling at home, and I believe the reason is the same. To illustrate the point I should like to read from the proceedings of the committee on travel trends at the 1956 convention of the Canadian tourist association. In the report there is the following:
There is another area where I suspect we are losing ground-
This refers to the loss of tourist business in Canada.
-although it is difficult to secure figures which will prove it. The areas to which I refer may be described as those playground areas immediately south of the border, just south of the border. Not only do these areas attract Canadian tourists and vacationers, but they also intercept much of the business which might otherwise find its way across the border right into Canada. It is with these areas that we must compete, at least in the near future, and to do so is a sizeable task. We must endeavour to match or better them in a type and decor of accommodation, the meals we serve, the hospitality we offer, the prices we charge, the recreational facilities and planned entertainment, and of utmost importance, the quality and quantity or roads of access from border points and between provinces and vacation areas in Canada.
We cannot expect full measure of success until we meet our competition with a product as good as or better than he is offering, nor until this is done, can we expect to receive full value for our advertising money which we spend seeking tourists to come to Canada or to stay in Canada and to spend their vacations here.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, it is no longer sufficient for the tourist industry and for our country to show our visitors nature's great beauties by day, and ask them to sleep in roadside cabins at night. The travelling public now wants the beauties of nature enhanced by modern buildings, neat gardens and conveniences. The short-term stay is increasing as a result of motor travel, and there are
2762	HOUSE OF
Loans to Tourist Resort Operators many more people touring the country staying by night at enjoyable sites, and perhaps only staying one, two or three days. It is to these people that we must offer accommodation which will be comfortable. It is not necessary for such accommodation to be anything more than comfortable. It can be rustic, as long as the tourist feels he has had a good place to stay, good meals and something which he could not get at home. It is only in that way that we can hope to hold the tourist business.
Our tourist operators are beginning to realize this difficulty. They want to modernize their accommodation. Recently the Canadian tourist association presented a brief to the Minister of Finance containing recommendations for the establishment of a fund similar to that which I am proposing today. Parts of this brief are very pertinent to this subject, so I should like to read a few paragraphs. These paragraphs deal entirely with the need of tourist operators for assistance in improving their plant, equipment and buildings. This is the quotation:
The tourist industry is composed mainly of small businesses. While the few larger establishments, such as the hotels and lodges of the transportation companies, are well known, the greater percentage of restaurants and accommodation establishments are small. Many are family enterprises.
Most of Canada's hotels, resorts and camps are 30, 40 and 50 years old. They were built when our national standard of living was not as high as it is today, when many hotels were not equipped with private baths or even running water in the rooms. At that time, the rooms were much smaller and were not furnished as comfortably as the travelling public expect and demand today.
Today's travellers are also demanding restaurants with the best decor, service and food. To meet this demand the modern restaurant must invest heavily in comfortable furnishings and labour-saving and sanitary equipment.
Most visitors come to Canada by automobile, and this mode of travel creates a greater demand for roadside accommodation of the highest quality. Although many motels have been built in recent years, a substantial percentage of Canada's motels and cabins need to be improved and enlarged.
The expansion and improvement of Canada's tourist establishments, which includes resorts, restaurants, hotels, motels and camps is urgently required. At present, the facilities which are inadequate and outmoded are being compared unfavourably with the more modern establishments which have been built in other countries in the past few years.
I believe that quotation sets out the situation so far as our business in Canada is concerned. Hon. members may say, if these people want to stay in business, what is wrong with them? Why are they not managing? Why are they not making sufficient income so the banks will assist them by way of loans? The answer is one of finances, and it is a rather basic problem.
In the first place, capital improvements cannot be made by these operators from the


moneys received during a season's operations. It is true that the establishments which have been making money in the past few years have been able to go to the bank in the spring and secure a loan to cover the cost of their summer improvements. In this way they can paint up and perhaps build a new fireplace, improve the dining room and so on. Then in the fall, when the season is over, they can repay the bank and have a little bit over on which to live during the winter. I am referring to the smaller establishments. The larger ones do not have this trouble because they are well established and have adequate finances behind them.
You may ask why the mortgage companies will not help these people. I feel there are two basic reasons. In the first place, the tourist business is a seasonal operation and is not classed as a good security or as a trust security by the mortgage companies. It is for this reason that a trust company or a mortgage company which handles trust funds cannot lend money to the tourist operators.
The reason for this is comparatively simple. A lot of these businesses are only as good as the man who operates them. He may have sufficient buildings and sufficient equipment, but if he is not a good operator he will lose money. While the mortgage companies may give a loan on a larger, well established business, when it comes to a smaller one these companies turn him down. As those with legal experience know, the terms of their mortgages do not prevent the owner from selling his property, provided the new purchaser undertakes payment. The mortgage is given, therefore, on the security of the land and buildings that the company finds there. If the company have to rely also on the integrity of the operator they may find themselves in difficulty. They are, therefore, very loath to grant loans to these people because of the fear that the operator, getting that much cash out of his business, may sell subject to the mortgage and someone could take over who might not operate the business in a satisfactory manner.
The mortgage companies do not like trouble, regardless of what some people may think. If they feel that they may run into difficulty on a loan, they would rather not grant it. This is what has happened on a good many of our smaller and medium-sized tourist businesses in Canada. I would say that the operators are completely unable to make improvements to their resorts because the bank can only lend money for the season, a six-month period, and the mortgage or trust company is unable to grant mortgages. These companies are not interested in whether or not this is a good thing for

Canada, and you cannot blame them because, after all, they are in business to make money. Our people who want mortgage money just cannot get it.
Many of these people realize that they have to make improvements. Perhaps they have some roadside cabins or a hotel or restaurant, the standard of which they would like to improve. So they make the effort; they go around from the banks to the mortgage companies trying to borrow money, and they cannot get it. So finally they decide, "Well, if I can't get the money I will just stay on here and get whatever I can out of this business, and not spend any money on it at all". As a result they leave their accommodation in the best condition in which they can put it and they get the odd three or four dollars from somebody who gets stuck on a heavy week end and finds there is no place to go.
I think that is a very bad advertisement for our country. There are not many of these people who wilfully withhold repairs. Most of them would like to make them but 'they cannot get the money. They just have to hang on. I feel that that is the basic cause of a good deal of our loss of the tourist industry. We are losing to overseas markets. We are losing to the United States. Those people are providing accommodation that people will stay in.
I should now like to speak for just a moment in connection with the financial proposal I have put forward in this motion. I am not suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that the form in which the motion is put forward is the final and absolute answer to the difficulty. After the subject has been discussed today and after it has been given some consideration it may be felt that there is some different way in which to help the tourist operators. But the proposition I should like to put forward is that the government give assistance to these people by somewhat the same method as national housing loans are made, where the lending company makes the loan and a certain proportion of the loan is guaranteed for repayment by the government.
This procedure would not cause any outlay in government funds until the point where they were called upon to make good the guarantee on a proposition which had become a loss. This is one proposal, and I think probably it is the best one, because the people who are willing to make these loans will go only so far. Even if they agree to make a loan they will go so far and they will say "Beyond that point we will not go".
The percentage in respect of the average house loan, I would say, in the case of the mortgage company will run anywhere between 40 per cent and 60 per cent of the
28. 1958
Loans to Tourist Resort Operators value of the residential property. But when it comes down to tourist property, if they lend at all it is not only at a high rate but the amount they will lend is very little more than 25 per cent of the value they place on the property. I would feel that the industry could be assisted if the mortgage companies were to make these advances in the percentage to what they would normally make if they were homes and if repayment could be guaranteed by the government.
Other propositions have been put forward to the government, Mr. Speaker. In 1956 the hotel association of Canada submitted a brief to the banking and commerce committee of the house, and at that time they suggested an amendment to the Industrial Development Bank Act by which the tourist business would be classed as an industry and some of the money available under the Industrial Development Bank Act could be given to the tourist industry. That is one suggestion.
This year, in 1958, the Canadian tourist association has suggested a tourist establishment improvement loan act. That is the suggestion from which I read a few moments ago. The tourist association would limit the loans to the improvement, replacement or expansion of existing resorts, restaurants, hotels, motels and camps. I stress the word "existing". Their proposal is that money should not be advanced to a new business. Their reasoning is that those who are in the tourist business and who have been reasonably successful in it will be able to take advantage of government loans and improve their properties and carry on. They suggest that the loss on such a project would be small, because those people who are in the business and who know it-and they admit that it is a seasonal business dependent on weather and a great many other factors-[DOT] can meet these conditions and know what to expect.
Of course we must understand that the Canadian tourist association is made up of associations already in existence, and that they are putting this suggestion forward on the basis that those in existence are the only people who can properly operate. I am not sure that I would be prepared to go all the way with that suggestion. However, there is some need for discretion and direction in the way the loans are made. They cannot be made to any person who decides he wants to go into the tourist business. It is too dangerous, risky and seasonal. When such a loan is made they must be satisfied that the person who is going to take it out can make the business pay under normal operating conditions.
That is the proposition that I intended to put forward, Mr. Speaker. To be fair, I think I should mention some of the objections to it,

Loans to Tourist Resort Operators and there have been objections. If there had not been objections the legislation would have been put through years ago.
The first objection that has been suggested to me is that if the operators cannot make sufficient money to run their business, why should the government step in and help them? In other words, if this is not a paying business why do they need help, and why should we spend public money to give it to them?
I think I have covered the answer. My answer to that question is first that the tourist business is of importance to Canada. The government plays very little part in the tourist business except to advertise it, but it is of very great importance in connection with our foreign dollars. That is the first answer. The second thing is that these people are in an unusual classification by reason of the type of business in which they are engaged. By and large they make money. If they did not make money there would not be so many of them going to Florida and setting up the adverse tourist balance that we already have. I do not think it is those people whom we need to help; I feel it is the smaller person who is struggling with a small business.
There is the second objection I have heard, namely that there are too many government subsidies, that everybody is getting a subsidy from the national treasury. Of course that is a very good answer. As far as I am personally concerned I think the less we interfere with private business, the better it is. To that extent I would agree with the objection. But again, here is a class of people who are, in effect, working for the government to bring money into the country. In so doing I feel that they merit some assistance, quite aside from the fact that they come third as a national income producer.
The third thing I should like to mention as an objection I have heard is this. I have read such objections in the newspapers and in reviews of this situation in other types of publications. It is said that this is a responsibility of the provinces rather than of the federal government.
The tourist business as it relates to a particular province has been very closely guarded by that province; for instance, the provinces do a certain amount of licensing and I know that in Ontario, for example, they have set up an act and a system of inspection which are intended to maintain standards. But I submit that this is a national problem; it is a problem which relates not to this or that province but to the whole country. A tourist coming to Ontario will probably go back to one of the United States or will go to Quebec or another province, and I think these people should be encouraged to stay in this country.

In this connection I would like to raise a few points respecting regulations in some of the provinces. In some provinces a tourist resort operator is told, "You will have to build new buildings, your buildings do not come up to standard. You will have to tear these down because we will not allow you to use them; they are in too bad shape." It is very difficult for a person to be placed in the position of being told he cannot stay in business, yet he cannot get any help. He is told, "You will have to fend for yourself or go out of business." Perhaps in some cases if his business is that bad it is as well that he go out of business, but a great proportion of such operators could carry on and keep their plant in good condition if they were given some assistance. I feel this is a joint responsibility between the federal and provincial governments, and that if some thinking were given to the matter along these lines it might produce beneficial results.
In conclusion I would like to say a few words about my particular riding and my own interest in this subject. While I have spoken in the house several times I have never made what might be called my maiden speech, because I have never had an opportunity to extol the virtues of Parry Sound and the Muskoka area. I would just like to say that the area which I represent includes all of the district of Parry Sound, all of the district of Muskoka and a major portion of Algonquin park.
It would be impossible to mention all the beautiful sections of this country lying between the Loring, Restoule, French river and lake Nipissing areas in the north to the Kahshe and Sparrow lake districts in the south, from the Georgian bay coast on the west to most of the Algonquin provincial park in the east. Georgian bay is, of course, one of the premiere tourist attractions in Canada, particularly for those interested in boating, and Algonquin park needs little introduction to anyone in this house. My riding also includes the Muskoka lakes chain, the lake of Bays and the Magnetawan river system, and thousands of smaller lakes and rivers in the tourist districts. It also includes the Parry Sound harbour area which has a rather unusual potential as a seaway port; but the importance of the area is shown in the fact that the national tourist industry is extremely well represented there. Mr. Dalton J. Caswell, the president of the hotel association of Canada, Mr. Ted Wright, president of the association of tourist resorts of Ontario, and Mr. George A. Martin, director of the Canadian tourist association, all operate resorts in the Parry Sound or Muskoka districts.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR JOINT LOANS TO TOURIST RESORT OPERATORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would indeed be remiss if at the very outset I did not say a word of congratulation to the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka for bringing in this notice of motion. I also congratulate him upon his well-chosen and well-delivered words which contain a lot of common sense and recommendations which I trust will be considered by this government. I also hope the government will take quick and justifiable action, and that the requests made will be granted as soon as possible.
Naturally, as a member of this house coming from Niagara Falls, which is the greatest tourist centre in the Dominion of Canada and indeed in the whole world, it might be expected that I would say something on this subject. As I have often said before, we are not jealous or selfish in any respect in my constituency. We like to share Niagara falls with the rest of the world, but we do appreciate its beauty as do our many visitors. In fact I had a dream about Niagara falls recently, and in it I was going up the steps to meet St. Peter-if a politician ever does get up the steps to meet St. Peter -and St. Peter asked me, "Houck, where do you come from?" I told him that I came from Niagara Falls and he said, "That is a very beautiful place, and I don't think you are going to like it here."
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, spoke about the Minister of Finance being one of the wonders of the world, but I would like to point out that we are known as one of the wonders of the world at Niagara Falls, and we would have to take that fact into due consideration before we would allow the minister's name to be added to the list. I think we are justifiably proud of the fact that the Princess Margaret has been fit to select Niagara Falls as one of the few places she will visit, and she will be there on Friday next. We are also very glad to know the Minister without Portfolio from Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) will accompany the princess when she visits Niagara Falls at that time.
As the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka has so ably stated, the Canadian tourist association has requested the Minister of Finance to submit to parliament a bill to establish a tourist establishment improve-rhent loan act, but I would like to say that I think this title is cumbersome though the request is pithy. I think the government at present in power should act quickly and should see what the association wants. I believe the requests made are reasonable
28, 1958
Loans to Tourist Resort Operators and would benefit not only the people catering to the tourist industry but the Canadian economy as a whole.
As was pointed out by the previous speaker, tourism is a major industry in our dominion, and I would like to emphasize the point made in the association's brief that only wheat and newsprint bring more money to this country than do our tourists. Furthermore, only newsprint brings more money to Canada from the United States than does the tourist industry. Tourism is big business in this country, but it is not as strong as it should be because all the people in this industry do not operate the sort of establishment which builds business. If they hope to improve their plants they must charge stiffer prices, which would mean discouraging business. The answer so far as I can see, and from what the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka said in this regard, would be a business loan. Such a loan, however, is generally difficult to obtain except at high interest rates.
I do not think the association is asking for a hand-out, but it does need a source from which it might borrow money-money which will be repaid but over a longer period and at easier interest rates. It is not asking for subsidization, but it does need help to improve facilities in order to attract more visitors, and that is what we want. We want to keep more Canadians from spending their money abroad, which is something they have been doing rather recklessly in recent years.
All this is simply good business for Canada. Wherever people travel they will buy, and that is why businessmen of all kinds in Canada stand to gain in terms of larger markets for their products if Canadians as well as overseas visitors are encouraged to travel in our dominion. If people do their travelling in this country this is where they will do their purchasing; it is as simple as that. There is a little-tapped source for greater prosperity in the fact that most Canadians still have not seen too much of their own country. Until recently more than one quarter of all adult Canadians had never seen any province beyond their own, yet two thirds of these same people had visited the United States.
Actually Canadians are the world's greatest travellers, and per capita they spend far more on travel outside their own country than do the people of any other nation. If we divide $441 million spent by Canadians outside Canada last year among 16 million, our population, we arrive at a figure of about $20.50 a head. Take the estimated billion and a half which Americans spend outside the United States and divide that by

Loans to Tourist Resort Operators the population of the United States, and the figure works out to something less than $10 a head.
Of the $441 million mentioned as Canadian expenditure outside Canada, $361 million represented the amount spent in the United States alone. Of this sum, $69 million represented purchases declared under the $100 customs exemption privilege for Canadians returning to Canada after an absence of 48 hours. This is actually a smaller percentage spent on duty free tourist imports than in previous years.
One reason for the popularity of foreign travel is, of course, advertising. It is becoming more and more apparent that at least in some parts of this country Canadians represent the fastest growing travel market in the world. For example, there are over 60 travel agencies in the city of Toronto, far more than can be found in a city of the same size in the United States. Cleveland, which is bigger than Toronto, had at the latest count only 23 travel agencies. While these travel merchants do help to sell Canada to Canadians, a greater part of their efforts must necessarily result in the sale of trips to far away places. This is not simply because commissions are greater on world cruises and flights to Florida than on smaller domestic tours, but also because the promoters of far away areas are very conscious of Canadian population centres as a source of tourist visitors and do everything in their power to help travel agents, transportation companies and other travel salesmen to send people their way.
As a result of years, perhaps decades, of promotion the trip abroad has been invested for Canadians with an aura of glamour. Many parts of Canada have glamour too, but no one has troubled to develop it in the minds of Canadians themselves. The Canadian government spends a million dollars or so on advertising to encourage United States residents to visit Canada's vacation attractions. In addition the provincial governments among them spend about another two million dollars. Of these provincial travel promotion dollars, four out of five are spent in the United States. Americans and others are being made aware by conscious effort of the pleasure and virtue of visiting Canada and knowing Canada better, but Canadians themselves are not. The fact that more than 28 million visits to Canada are made annually, seven or eight million of them for extended periods, attests rather obviously to the fact that we do have very real attractions for tourists. It is simply that we are not conscious of them ourselves.

An impressive example of what tourism can mean to Canadian industry was recently given to the Pembroke, Ontario, Kiwanis club by C.T.A. president W. Gordon Wood. Speaking on April 28 Mr. Wood said:
About 7,500,000 Americans came into Canada by car to stay for more than two days last year. If each one of these visitors had been induced to remain just another 15 or 20 minutes to buy a fried egg sandwich, they would have consumed an extra 625,000 dozen eggs, 750,000 loaves of bread and 120,000 pounds of butter.
Don't ever let a farmer say that the tourist industry does not mean anything to him. Tourism benefits everybody.
Then the Minister of Finance, and the minister of northern affairs spoke at the tourist convention held in Ottawa in 1957 and made some very encouraging remarks to that convention to the effect that they, in their official positions, would do anything they could to help the tourist business in Canada; that they realized the obstacles the industry had to face and felt that the industry should be encouraged, and that this encouragement should be supported by some definite action.
In dollar volume, tourism is Canada's third largest industry. It is big business, and it is the aim of the C.T.A. to make it bigger business. No dollar gets into circulation as quickly as the tourist dollar, which is distributed over and over again until it reaches everyone's pocketbook. The wholesaler, distributor, banker, jobber and manufacturer, the butcher, baker and, yes, even the undertaker, benefit from travel, whether from within or without Canada. Tourists add to our tax collections. This means better roads, better schools and a better estate for all Canadians.
And let me tell hon. members that no business is as furiously competitive as the international travel market. The world is now living on one Main street. No land is remote any more. To meet this competition Canada must increase her promotion and improve her plant. The small operators in the tourist business cannot do this by themselves. In Great Britain bankers, industrialists and businessmen have thrown their weight behind the travel industry. Tourists now earn more dollars for Britain than any other business. But Canada, despite its proximity to the world's richest nation, is losing its share of the travel market, as the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka so rightly pointed out.
I wish to add that in my opinion the Canadian tourist association was right when it asked the government of Canada to take action which would relieve the Canadian tourist industry of the very serious disability caused by the lack of financial credit, and thus make it possible for our tourist industry, through expansion and modernization, to

compete effectively in the world tourist market. In its request for assistance the C.T.A. submitted three points for consideration with regard to the travel industry, as follows:
1.	Through travel from other countries it is the source of new found money which creates additional commerce and employment in Canada.
2.	An efficient, attractive tourist "plant" in this country can hold travelling Canadians in Canada and keep in circulation here money which would otherwise be lured abroad.
3.	Travel by Canadians within Canada promotes a deeper understanding of our own country and a greater appreciation of our land and our rich heritage, and it fosters national unity.
The association also pointed out to the cabinet that the important addition made to Canada's wealth from tourist income is unusual in three ways:
1.	It causes very little depletion in our natural resources.
2.	It sells our goods and services without our having to pay the cost of transporting them to market. The "market" pays its own way here.
3.	It benefits almost every phase of our general economy.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should just like to place a few figures on the record. In 1951 the average spending per person per trip was just under $49. In 1952 that expenditure increased to $62.25, and today it is almost $70. One thing is very important. In order to increase the success of our tourist business we must increase the length of time tourists spend in our country. Some 75 per cent of our tourists spend less than four days here, yet about 73 per cent of our visitors have between 14 and 20 days annual vacation.
Only 10 per cent of our visitors spend from two to three weeks in this country. If we could only induce those who at present spend only one day with us to increase their stay by two more days, it would increase our tourist business by at least 15 per cent. A survey shows that out of the United States tourist dollar 11.6 cents is spent on gas and oil, car repairs and transportation generally; 49.4 cents is spent on accommodation and food; 35 cents is spent on consumer purchases, and 7 cents on licences for fishing and hunting, boats, and so on.
Mr. Speaker, I am very serious about the point I am about to make now, and I think I have a right to bring up this subject. I have often heard it said by Canadians-and I think it is to be regretted that it has been said-that "the Yanks" are crude and boastful and that the United States opinion of us is similar. Nothing can be further from the truth. Generalities are always dangerous and usually founded on half-truths from unreliable sources; certainly they are ill-considered opinion. I am sure that every clear-cut, right-thinking Canadian agrees with me that
Loans to Tourist Resort Operators such statements about our friends from the great republic are utter nonsense. Most Canadians like the people of the United States, and I can assure you that most Americans have a high regard for us as well.
Disraeli once said over 100 years ago, "It is much easier to be critical than to be correct." He also said that individualities may form communities but it is institutions alone that create a nation. I have found through my experience in Niagara Falls in talking to tourists that one of the things our United States visitors complain most about is that in certain sections of our country we are too much Americanized. On many and many an occasion I have heard it said that some Canadian businessmen fly the American stars and stripes on every occasion in order, as they think, to lure the United States trade.
Nothing could be farther from the truth. The reason many people visit the United States or Canada is not that they want to see the same things they could walk down their own main street and see but they want to see Canadians as they live, as they act, as they work and as they really are. I am for things Canadian. To me a Canadian is a person of manners and people with manners do not go around insulting their neighbours, let alone their best customers.
The United States government is certainly to be congratulated because with its recent customs exemptions it has been doing everything possible to assist our tourist industry. United States residents may now take back, once every 31 days, merchandise for personal or household use to the value of $200, duty and tax free, provided that resident has remained in Canada more than 48 hours. An additional exemption of $300, which makes a total of $500 duty and tax free, is allowed once every six months if the resident has been in Canada more than 12 days.
Residents of the United States visiting Canada for less than 48 hours may take back, for personal or household use, merchandise to the value of $10, duty and tax free. Such exemptions must not include more than 50 cigarettes, 10 cigars, one quarter pound of manufactured tobacco, four ounces of alcoholic beverages or four ounces of alcoholic perfumes, whatever that might be. Gift packages may also be sent to the United States if they are plainly marked "gift" and the value indicated if the aggregate value of the articles received by a person in one day does not exceed $10.
The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka spoke about his riding, and I should like to say a few words about my riding and my experience with tourist
2768	HOUSE OF
Loans to Tourist Resort Operators operators in that area. In the first place, many tourist operators have a short season, with a few exceptions who operate all year round and who generally have some connection or work in a commercial trade to keep them going. Most of the tourist operators in Niagara Falls calculate their season from May 1 to November 1. They reason that if they have not made any money by then they will not make any at all. Naturally, as was pointed out by the hon. member who introduced the resolution, the farther north you go the shorter the season, unless the operators there promote such activities as skiing.
We normally figure that about 6 million people visit Niagara Falls during the year, including those attending conventions. The regrettable fact about this is that only about 10 per cent of these 6 million visitors to Niagara Falls remain overnight. In other words, I do not think we need any more people to visit Niagara Falls, but we should do and are doing everything possible to persuade these people to come and stay overnight. That is where the actual money is, and that is when it reaches the local merchants.
Using all available accommodation in Niagara Falls we can bed down about 7,000 people each night, but I must admit that one of our biggest headaches is the provision of more modern accommodation. It is true that within the past 10 years tourist accommodation has grown in our city by nearly 80 per cent, but I am sorry to say there are still many establishments which could or should be torn down and replaced by up to date services. It is also true that the owners of such establishments spent every cent they could get while they were in the money instead of laying it away for replacements. In the meantime the newer establishments which have been erected have so many improvements that the cost for each new unit runs from $6,000 to $10,000, including equipment, whereas originally some of the cabins would have cost perhaps less than $1,000 had they been constructed 10 years ago or more.
Many of the tourist establishments have good locations but poor conveniences, and these would be the ones which might utilize any loan provision. Some of our up to date motels in Niagara Falls could be greatly improved or extended if more money were available to them. Normally it takes a tourist establishment from three to five years before it begins to get repeat business, and these three to five years are the danger years. Certainly the industrial development bank does a good job for industry and a similar


plan for tourism might be feasible, though it is my belief that the controls would have to be pretty well defined.
In the case of industry there is usually a past history which could be used as a guide, but in the case of a tourist establishment the tourist business is relatively too new to enable one to design the same kind of code. Unfortunately many of the people entering the tourist business have had no experience and have never demonstrated an ability to conduct a motel on a businesslike basis. They would be the greatest headache of the government in considering a tourist loan program. Certainly with the federal and other levels of government making grants and other provisions for municipal development such as those for hospitals, education, etc., there is no reason in the world why this government should not consider making grants to the tourist industry, as it is one of the most economical to operate.
This year in Niagara Falls has been an unusual one from our standpoint. Our chamber of commerce reception office and that of the Ontario government has received fewer inquiries over the counter than in previous years. Mail inquiries are also down to some extent, though not as much as personal inquiries. In spite of this, however, the bridge figures are higher and cars entering the park are more numerous than last year. One can enter the park on almost any day during the tourist season and find cars bearing license plates from every state in the United States and every province in Canada.
This year people seem to be skimping on meals, the purchase of souvenirs, etc., but interestingly enough-and at the same time difficult to understand-our most expensive overnight accommodation seems to be at a premium. We in Niagara Falls have increased the tempo of our publicity and have attempted to advertise our more up to date establishments. Perhaps because of the fact that we are a tourist centre in Niagara Falls, private capital would be easier to obtain than in the northern areas.
I wish now to sum up the remarks I have made. I would reiterate that in the first place the tourist business is much more fickle and much more difficult to assess than is ordinary industry. It depends upon location, the services provided, unemployment and other factors which are not so important with respect to regular industry.
In the second place, if the government establishes a loan system a person who applies for assistance should have some record of a successful business operation, either as a tourist operator or in some related line.

In the third place, there is a great demand for improved facilities, and although people may seem to skimp on some expenses they do appear to want modern, comfortable accommodation.
In the fourth place, the tourist business in Canada generally needs improvement in order to successfully compete with our competitors in various other countries. I would remind the house, though, that much improvement could be shown in other fields as well, such as courtesy and meals.
In the fifth place, I would remind hon. members that the tourist industry is one of the cheapest to operate, yet is a very lucrative source of income for the entire country.
May I say, as I said at the beginning, that I hope this government will take cognizance of the motion presented so well today by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. I trust it will be only a matter of a short space of time until we will hear it announced that the government will extend this assistance to an industry which so greatly requires it. I would remind hon. gentlemen opposite that the government has boasted that it would lend assistance to small business. Tourism is a big business, but it relates to and affects 90 per cent of the small businesses in this country. If the government will come to the assistance of the tourist industry many small businesses will be helped, and the Canadian economy will receive an uplift as well. I remember my leader's platform in the last campaign, that we would help small business as much as possible. This is one of the things we would have done. Therefore I plead with the government to give some recognition to what has been said by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken). Let us not talk out the motion but rather let us have action by the government.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR JOINT LOANS TO TOURIST RESORT OPERATORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join with the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Houck) in congratulating the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) for bringing this motion before us. It is often difficult to avoid a repetition in the house when there is a division of opinion but it is almost impossible to avoid repetition when we are apparently in complete accord and, perhaps more important, when some of us have done our homework from the same general report for which I think we should thank the Canadian tourist association.
I should like at this particular time, because I think it is appropriate when a great many people are returning from their holidays, to add a word or two not by way of statistical evidence but as to the general
28, 1958	2769
Loans to Tourist Resort Operators need, so ably put forward by my good friend, the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. I think that perhaps I would not be accused of repetition if I were to accept as read his case for the necessity for a motion and eventually legislation of this type, but rather deal with the forecast of the potential that we may expect yet even this year and what we may anticipate as well in the years to come.
The fact that we may be losing part of our opportunity to develop this industry has been placed before us in no uncertain terms. In Great Britain the tourist industry is regarded as its most important. In the United States, as has been stated, it is second and in the case of Canada it is exceeded in gross dollars only by wheat and agriculture. Forecasts of what we may expect present an even more interesting comparison in that this year it is anticipated that 2.6 million carloads of United States visitors alone will stay more than 48 hours in Canada and will spend some $350 million on goods and services. In my own city of Calgary it was estimated that in a 90-day period recently they spent some $5 million in that growing centre of the tourist industry. In addition it is anticipated that this year transportation companies will spend another $4 million in advertising and promoting the tourist industry. The government of Canada already has an appropriation of slightly over $1.2 million for the purpose of advertising the advantages of Canada to anyone who wishes to visit our country as a tourist.
The question before us, Mr. Speaker, is how we can best back up that investment, for I think we will have to concede that there is no point in spending this amount of money if we are not prepared first of all to accept the challenge that competition is growing stronger for the tourist dollar throughout the world and, second, that it is no longer sufficient for us simply to make use of posters in a number of countries pointing out the advantages to be gained by visiting Canada unless we are able to provide the entertainment and type of visit these people are going to expect.
We have made a great deal of headway. At long last most of our provinces have recognized the need for improved roads. Many of our provinces have at long last recognized that social changes require more lenient liquor privileges. Many of our provinces have recognized the need for more uniformity in traffic signs and signals. So we come down to the last problem, that of the accommodation plant, whether it be one of the 3,000 motels or whether it be one of the major hotels in our hotel system which house the people who come to our country.

Loans to Tourist Resort Operators
It has been shown that to put up a motel based on minimum standards and with perhaps 10 to 12 rooms requires an investment of something in the order of $100,000 or about $6,000 to $8,000 per unit. You can find any number of requests at the chartered banks by individual businessmen and women who have applied for loans either on a short or long term basis and have been refused or had their requests only partially granted because of the limiting factor that the tourist industry has been considered to be only a seasonal industry. The limitation imposed by the chartered banks is no fault of theirs but is one of the requirements under which they are permitted to operate but nonetheless the limitation prevents these individual businessmen and women not only from building and reconstructing but from improving the facilities they now have.
There are, of course, a variety of methods by which the problem I now present can be solved. They have been enunciated by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. The generality of the resolution refers to one method. A system by which we can create wider or more generous provisions for the chartered banks so far as lending is concerned is another. A third, which has been suggested on many occasions, is the utilization of the industrial bank. I think that in principle most members will agree that the industrial bank should deal with the larger borrower, one who is undertaking something of a more substantial nature than an individual hotel or motel.
I am going to leave the case for improving the plant or facilities for a moment to introduce a new thought and to take some of the responsibility for improving the facilities and the methods by which we attract people to Canada off the shoulders of the government and place it on the shoulders of the operators themselves and, in fact, the Canadian public at large. I think that most of us who have looked at this motion have regarded it favourably but with this reservation. How far is the government expected to go in underwriting, subsidizing, supporting financially, giving outright grants to or interfering with a particular business or industry? I am one of those who believe that regardless of political party we are inclined to go too far in this day and age in endeavouring to provide assistance to bail out people, assistance which was never intended to be within the means of the free enterprise system under which we live today.
I think where you find the line of demarcation, and this is the reason that I can lend unqualified support to this motion, is that the government should give consideration

to helping those who are prepared to help themselves on the basis that this money will be returned with interest, but most important on the basis of creating a better understanding between Canadians and of providing facilities which, in themselves, are going to create increased revenues within Canada which will circulate within Canada. All this will build up, as has been pointed out, the second most important industry in our country, and these are firm bases for support of this motion.
I do not not wish to deviate from the point I want to make here. This is not the responsibility of the government alone. We find many of our operators who regard the tourist as something essential only to have a bed occupied, and can hardly wait to have the occupant replaced by yet another tourist in order to collect yet another fee. Fortunately these people are in the minority. Too often we find the services or facilities which are offered are inclined to be restrictive, and not because of the shortage of income. Too often our own Canadian people, and we are no exception in this regard amongst the other countries in the world, are inclined not to realize that they, as individuals, benefit from every tourist who comes to Canada. The moneys which are given directly to the tourist industry filter back into the pockets of the ordinary citizen. The principle of making the tourist welcome so that he will want to come back is still, in my opinion, in relation to this motion the most important quality that we will have to instil into Canadians.
Now, I have had my share of opportunity to travel throughout Canada. In the context in which I have already spoken, one of the most important areas in which we can improve this industry is by showing some imagination. We have developed a number of centres which contain tourist attractions, Muskoka, Niagara Falls, the Calgary Stampede, the great Shakespearean festival at Stratford, the great areas of the maritimes. These centres add much to the imagination of Canadians who realize that they are indeed lucrative sources of income. We, in Calgary as an example, some years ago introduced the white hat. Unfortunately, the other areas of Canada with less imagination have also seen fit to adopt it as their national headgear. Anybody west of the great lakes today is referred to as a Calgarian, regardless of whether or not he wears a white hat, but invariably he does. I think the point I would make is that imagination and initiative to develop ideas, to develop entertainment and attractions, must come from the people themselves so that we will establish what has been described heretofore as a national character.

The people from Europe and the United States do not come to Canada to see us copy a particular type of individual or type of country; they expect we will be different. They expect to see something that will identify us as Canadians and not as a carbon copy of any other country. I suggest that one of the most important things towards which the Canadian tourist association has been working has been not only the improvement of the plant and its operations, but also the frame of mind in which Canadians would recognize the importance of this industry to their own welfare as such they can feel they are a part of this industry. As I said at the outset, we should make the tourist want to come back.
The motion calls for an improved system of providing loans, and I had intended to go into the method by which this could be done. However, that has been so ably covered by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka that my remarks would only be superfluous. Let me say that there is another area, that of the larger institution in the larger centre which has a potential to draw the tourist and which must also be given consideration. It could come within the confines of this motion, but perhaps it might be more adapted to a widening of the provisions of the industrial bank. I would also like to compliment my colleague, the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Houck), on his very fine contribution to this debate. I am very pleased to be able to assure the house that in my province we are much more aesthetic in our approach to the tourist industry than appears to be the case on the mainland. We do not entice people to stay another hour or so or to eat another 600,000 eggs, nor do we entice them to spend another few million dollars. We like them to stay with us because we like people; we are friendly and sociable and we enjoy their company. We want them to enjoy us and furthermore we like them to drink in our natural beauty and to enjoy the pleasure of our outdoor life, which is second to none in this country. Of course if in the process they do spend a few more millions or eat a few more eggs that is all to the good but it is purely incidental.
Those hon. members who had the pleasure of seeing the pictures shown in the committee room last Tuesday, I believe through the courtesy of Senator Pratt, will realize that in Newfoundland we do have very fine tourist attractions. Those hon. members who were unfortunate enough to have missed those pictures will, I hope, have another opportunity in the near future, because I understand there was sufficient interest aroused to request a second showing. As those pictures prove, we do have unsurpassed tourist attractions in the way of hunting for both big and small game, fresh water fishing, boating and deep sea fishing. The opportunity to develop our tourist industry, was, in fact, one of the main arguments put forward in favour of confederation, and to that end the terms of union embodied a provision that the trans-Canada highway should cross the province from one end to the other and that when this route was completed a new and modern car ferry would be built by the federal government and put into service on the Cabot strait. The vessel designed for this service is the William

Carson, and we understand from what the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) told us a few weeks ago that it will undertake this service some time in the middle of next month.
The delay has been somewhat of a blessing in disguise, because the tourist industry in Newfoundland cannot prosper until we have sufficient accommodation available for the tourists. That is our greatest need at the present time, but in spite of the lower interest rate tight money still exists as far as the tourist industry is concerned. The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka gave us some of the reasons why this should be the case, and I think that since this is a national question it is right for the industry to expect some assistance from the federal government.
The industry is not asking for a handout; it is asking for credit which cannot be obtained from the usual sources because of conditions which apply to the tourist industry more than to other industries. The season is short; business takes a long time to become established, and there are, even now, better investment opportunities. There is a definite need here which must be met, and in Newfoundland, and in my own riding in particular, the tourist industry has practically come to a standstill because of the lack of accommodation.
Efforts have been made by the provincial government during the last four years, but because of conditions on the money market these efforts have not been successful, and unless funds are made available to people who are willing to risk money of their own in these ventures, the tourist industry cannot develop as it could properly be expected to develop.
Nevertheless, it seems to me that this industry has today become almost an essential industry; it is certainly an industry of national importance and one which makes a great contribution to both the national economy and the provincial economy not only through the money which visitors spend directly but because of the encouragement which is given to the development of small home industries.
It is now not uncommon for the government to make money available to assist industries which private capital is not prepared to develop, and certainly the tourist industry has a very strong claim for assistance. As the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka has pointed out, the method by which this money is made available is not important; it is the principle which is important, and I hope that the government will recognize the principle embodied in this resolution and, before long, embody it in the laws and statutes of this country.
