Mr. Speaker, the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of introducing legislation to authorize the making of loans, jointly with an approved lending institution, to tourist resort operators for the purpose of constructing or making capital improvements to tourist accommodation.
This is, I feel, an excellent one, and most timely. I was deeply interested in this resolution when I saw it on the order paper because I have spent all my life in a province which is very tourist conscious. I refer of course, to New Brunswick, which has been called the picture province of the dominion. It has been said by previous speakers that the tourist industry is big business, and that is quite true. That is borne out by figures which have been given, but which, I feel, bear repetition. In 1948 the money which came into this country as a result of this industry amounted to $280 million; by 1957 it had risen to $362 million.
Since the end of the second world war travel has grown from being a luxury of the wealthy few to being an accepted way of life for every portion of the North American population. The increase in wages and salaries, the shorter working week and longer paid holidays have put the travelling vacation within the reach of everyone. Tourism has reached the status of a major industry. In addition to the moneys spent in Canada by visitors from foreign lands, millions of Canadians spend hundreds of millions of dollars every year travelling in Canada. Tourism has a special significance for the Canadian economy and society in three ways:
1.	Through travel from other countries it is the source of new found money which creates additional commerce and employment in Canada.
2.	An efficient, attractive tourist "plant" in this country can hold travelling Canadians in Canada and keep in circulation here money which would otherwise be lured abroad.
3.	Travel by Canadians within Canada promotes a deeper understanding of our own country and a greater appreciation of our land and our rich heritage, and it fosters national unity.
Tourism means much to Canada, but it could mean a great deal more if the tourist industry were more adequately equipped to meet competition in the international market. In the United States, for example, the tourist business in 1956 grossed about two-thirds as much as the whole agricultural and livestock industry, according to the United States department of commerce. If this trend continues, tourism in the United States may soon surpass agriculture as a major industry.
2776	HOUSE OF
Loans to Tourist Resort Operators
Obviously, with more potential tourists than ever before, tourism could be very much bigger business in Canada. But under existing conditions Canada is not holding its own, because last year we had a deficit of $161 million in our tourist account. In other words, while those visiting Canada-and these are dominion bureau of statistics figures-spent $362 million, Canadian visitors to the United States and other countries abroad spent $523 million, a deficit of $161 million which is approximately the same figure as in 1956. It has gone up from a balance, on the other side of the ledger, since 1948, of $145 million.
Canada formerly received the largest share of the money which residents of the United States spent in visiting other countries but that is no longer the case. Since 1953 Europe has attracted more United States dollars through visiting tourists than Canada has. Despite the increase in the cost of transportation, spending by United States travellers in all countries outside the United States is almost double since 1949 but during that same period United States spending in Canada increased by only 23 per cent while Canadian expenditure in the United States rose by 144 per cent.
Many reasons can be given for these travel trends. Among the most important and the more obvious in this competition are the romance of distant areas, the speed of modern air travel, the premium on the Canadian dollar about which I should like to speak later, and the comforts offered by facilities abroad. Competition for the Canadian and United States travel dollar will increase as the world shrinks and as North Americans take more to the motor car and as we, as a people, grow more curious about the world itself. This makes it imperative that Canadians who cater to tourists be able to offer the very best services and facilities to those who demand them when they come here.
It is, of course, sound business practice to improve tourist facilities and accommodation. Millions of dollars are being spent every year by governments, transportation companies and other businesses by way of large advertising campaigns inviting our neighbours in that great country to the south of us to visit Canada and inviting Canadians to travel in Canada. Last year the Canadian government travel bureau spent more than $1,200,000 on an excellent promotion campaign in the United States. I believe that it is economic to back up this expenditure with a product of the highest quality. Promotion of this type abroad and improvement to the tourist plant at home are inseparable. Good advertising alone will not sell an inferior product.


We must offer the traveller more when he gets here. We want him to enjoy the longest possible vacation in Canada and, even more important, to return another year with his friends.
I feel that one of the major deterrents to improvement in tourist facilities and accommodation is the lack of credit facilities. The tourist industry needs long term credit at a reasonable rate of interest. Loans of this nature are not readily available from the chartered banks, insurance companies and trust companies. Without long term credit at moderate interest rates, the return on investment in the tourist industry, especially in the seasonal establishments, is not high enough to allow for the extensive upgrading which is required. The prices charged by the older establishments are low in comparison with those charged by newer places and yet, for what many operators have to offer, the rates are perhaps all that the service is worth. Most of these operators realize that their facilities should be improved and they are anxious to carry out a modernization program but they lack the needed resources. Should an operator improve his facilities by borrowing other than from a bank, insurance company or trust company, he is often obliged to pay a bonus of 10 per cent to 12 per cent and interest payments of eight to 10 per cent or higher. He is then forced to charge very high prices in order to be able to repay the loan in the allotted time. This situation gives the tourist industry a bad name and decreases Canada's competitive position in the industry.
In a recent brief presented to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) the Canadian tourist association advocated that this government should enact legislation to be known as the "tourist establishment improvement loan act". The resolution now being discussed follows along that line. I should like to place on the record the recommendations of the association with respect to the provisions of the proposed act:
Such an act should provide:
(a)	Moneys for the improvement, replacement and expansion of established resorts, restaurants, hotels, motels and camps.
(b)	A maximum on individual loans of not less than $50,000.
(c)	A maximum term of not less than 10 years.
(d)	Loans to be made at a reasonable rate of interest, not to exceed the prevailing rate at the chartered banks.
(e)	Funds to be made available by means of government guaranteed loans through the chartered banks.
(f)	Total amount to be guaranteed by the government of Canada, not less than $15 million.
The Canadian tourist association is the authority on this particular phase of our economy and it is interesting to consider what

it feels the adoption of these provisions would accomplish. The brief states that in the opinion of the Canadian tourist association the adoption of these provisions would reduce the risk factor of the lending program in two ways:
(i)	The operation of tourist enterprises requires specialized knowledge and techniques. It is therefore prudent to guarantee loans only to persons who are established in the industry and have demonstrated success.
The hon. member for Parry Sound-Mus-koka (Mr. Aiken) made that point very well but I feel it bears repetition. The brief continues with these words:
The risk of lending to inexperienced operators, who might fail in business, is therefore minimized.
(ii)	Lending through the chartered banks would also minimize the risk factor. The manager of the local bank knows local conditions, and he is in the best position to assess the credit worthiness of the client-to assess his record as an operator and the improvements which are contemplated.
I feel that a loan of this type would have beneficial results beyond the improvement of many individual tourist establishments. It would assist in making Canada's tourist industry more competitive in the world market. It would generate new income which would ease Canada's international trade deficit, especially with the United States. It would support our extensive travel promotion program in other countries. It would provide construction and employment during the fall and winter months when seasonal unemployment is at its peak. It would stimulate every phase of the national economy.
The question was raised when the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) was speaking about how long the tourist industry had been a factor in our economy. I can well remember as a very young lad on the Restigouche river in northern New Brunswick-that river which is famous all over the world for its Atlantic salmon, the finest fighting fish in the world-United States sportsmen who came up there summer after summer and who had been coming for years. Their contribution to the economy of that particular region was one of the most important factors in the livelihood of many of the people there. I had a personal interest in it because, as a young teacher in a community on that river, 90 per cent of my salary was paid by the United States sportsmen. I began to realize how much the Atlantic salmon was worth to the people there.
I feel, however, that we in Canada who are interested in the tourist industry-while most of us have no direct connection with it yet we are interested in the economy of the nation and the financial betterment of our country-have missed the boat badly in

Take, for example, in the matter of food served. There is perhaps no finer dish in the world than a freshly boiled lobster recently taken from the sea off St. Andrew's or somewhere else in the east, or perhaps steamed clams or Atlantic salmon. But what do we see served so frequently in many Canadian restaurants? Southern fried chicken! I do not believe that visitors from the United States have come to Canada to enjoy southern fried chicken. I feel they would enjoy much more a St. Andrew's lobster or Atlantic salmon or some other fine Canadian dish. I could continue at some length but I need only say that all of us have had the unfortunate experience of eating in restaurants where the food has been poorly prepared and served although in all fairness I must say that many of our eating establishments are adequate.
As I have driven about the country-and in the last few years I have seen much of Canada-I have been amazed at the number of hotels and motels that are located right beside the road. Perhaps here in Ottawa where there are several fine motels that is necessary but when I go to bed at night I like to be located some distance from the road so my sleep is not disturbed by traffic and street noise. Many people do not seem to give any thought to the location of the tourist accommodation they construct. Perhaps the only thought they have is the cheapness of the land. I think a great mistake is made in this respect.
There is another thing about which I should like to speak very briefly. I think we miss the boat again with respect to the service that is provided in so many of the hotels, motels and restaurants in this country that cater to our people. I do not think there is any substitute for courtesy and cleanliness. At the 1957 annual meeting of the Canadian tourist association it was suggested by one of the panelists that there should be a school for those people who are in this type of service and I can quite appreciate that. As a teacher deeply interested for most of my life in education and teaching others certain skills, I think that is an excellent idea. For example, I think waitresses should be taught that it is not necessary to insert the whole thumb into a bowl of soup but only up to the first knuckle, and other things like that. In a more serious vein, I believe there certainly is scope for improvement in this direction. Too many times it seems to me that restaurant operators, motel operators and others seem to get their help from the cheapest possible source. That

Loans to Tourist Resort Operators may be so; I do not know. But I think if more care were exercised in hiring and training staff it might help.
I come now to another point with respect to which many will perhaps disagree. I think one of the curses of travel is that degrading habit known as tipping. I am told that some 100 or so years ago the word "tip" originated when a box was placed in Lloyds restaurant * at the beginning Lloyds was a coffee house before it became a great insurance firm- with the words "to insure promptness", and from that the word "T-I-P" evolved. On the other hand I have read that thousands of years ago this same practice was in effect. How many times in our travels, have we received poor service and yet have been expected to tip the person who has performed some service for us for which they have already been paid a salary?
I had occasion a few years ago to travel to Vancouver and to stay for a short time at one of the luxury hotels of the west. I do not do that very often because I never felt I could afford it. But in this particular instance in getting from the train to the hotel and then from the hotel back to the train I ransomed my luggage several times from the young lads who carried it. The president of the Canadian tourist association, W. Gordon Wood, who is also vice-president of sales for T.C.A., had this to say about tipping at the 1957 convention of the association:
Perhaps the time has come for us to consider the establishment of a committee to study the abolition of tipping. We are not saying that this is practical-
I think it is practical.
-or whether it is right or wrong-
Personally I feel it is wrong.
-but we *i know this-
This is the point made by this man who is very conversant with tourist affairs in general.
__that if Canada could announce to the United
States tomorrow that we have abolished all forms of tipping, we believe that we could wipe out our travel deficit.
That deficit, as I said earlier, is now $361 million a year. I believe that people who perform a service, whether as a porter on a railway train or as a waitress in the parliamentary restaurant, should be paid a salary commensurate with the work they do. I do not and never have believed in the practice of tipping because I feel it is degrading.
There is another point I wish to put forward and it is strange it has never been mentioned before. I refer to the handling of United States money in our country. When United States tourists come to the border no attempt is made to change their currency

into Canadian currency. A Canadian or anyone else travelling in France would very soon obtain French francs. A person travelling in England would immediately obtain his pounds, shillings and pence or his "quid" and "bob". But when United States tourists come to this country no such attempt is made.
What do we find? We find that because of economic factors their money is not worth as much as ours. The result is that time after time in our establishments we see arguments going on between some poor harassed cashier and a United States tourist because their dollar is only worth 96 cents. We have all had the experience in the past-I know I can remember it as as a youngster-of going across the border to the United States, having our money thrown back to us and being told that it was no good. Possibly that still happens. I do not know. But I believe it would be a very sensible thing for the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, the Department of Citizenship and Immigration or whatever department is concerned, to have at the larger border crossing points at least, the necessary facilities so that as soon as these people have been checked through by customs and immigration officials they can change their money into Canadian money. Then they would have the currency of our country as long as they were here and there would not be these arguments and hard feeling-there is hard feeling when United States tourists find that their money is not worth as much as ours.
Going back to my youth many years ago I can well remember living with a farmer who had a rather good mixed farm. He had done well and I asked him what was the secret of his success. He said, "My boy, on a farm like this the whole year round you have always got to have something to sell." I think that in Canada we have a great deal to sell if we package it properly.
Like other members who have spoken today, and as I will perhaps be the only speaker from the province of New Brunswick, I should like to take a few moments to tell about the beauties of my province and what it has to offer to the visitor. I am sure many hon. members have never been that far east. There is the beauty of the Restigouche, Miramichi and Saint John rivers, perhaps second to none on the whole North American continent, -the tidal bore of the Petitcodiac, the reversing falls on the Saint John river, the only phenomenon of its kind in the world the Magnetic Hill, the beauty of the islands of the bay of Fundy such as Grand Manan and Campobello. In fact, so beautiful is Campo-bello that for much of his life the late President Franklin Delano Roosevelt spent his

summers there and, some say, loved it even more than his own country.
There is the beauty of the historic sites, the land that Cartier first saw in 1534, that was first settled in 1604 and to which the Loyalists came when they emigrated to this country. I could talk for many hours about the beauty of the province from which I come. I simply suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to all other members that at the earliest opportunity you come to visit us in New Brunswick. I am sure you will receive a welcome second to none in the whole country.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding what was said by the hon. member for Port Arthur, I feel that the resolution of the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka is not socialism. It is merely justice. If it is implemented, and I am sure it will be at some time by this government in its wisdom, and it possesses a great deal of wisdom, it will be a great boon to this most important phase of the life of our country.

Mr. Speaker, a country like Canada which has a very considerable trade deficit with its neighbours to the south should, in order to balance its payments, make the greatest effort to promote the tourist industry, as one of the most efficient means to balance our country's trade deficit. In practically all spheres of our economic activity, the tourist industry acts as a stimulus. Let tourists come over in large numbers and it means more business for hotels, restaurants and, therefore, all who supply food products and services.
There are, of course, areas in Canada that are just about perfectly set up for that pur-
2782	HOUSE OF
Loans to Tourist Resort Operators pose. Indeed, in such areas, the tourist trade is so profitable that in some cases it can be said that it is their chief industry. However, Canada as a whole is far from being perfectly organized in this respect, and there are still large areas which, though extremely picturesque, do not benefit from the economic help this very modern industry could bring them. Why? Because lack of capital has prevented the building of essential accommodation that would draw and hold visitors here. One case in point is my own riding, though I shall not attempt at this time to describe all its features and attractions. Of course, we have first class hotels and restaurants, but just enough to accommodate commercial travellers or businessmen. To open up the kingdom of Saguenay to large scale tourism, several million dollars should be invested in specialized accommodation, and our businessmen lack the required capital to finance such a project on their own.
Until about 10 years ago, the only tourists who came over would sail up the Saguenay in a Canada Steamship Line vessel and used the boat as a hotel even when it put in at Chicoutimi. This is a type of tourists who are profitable only to the steamship company. As for our railway, to which I have referred on a previous occasion, it is far from being the modern, twentieth century transport which is likely to attract visitors to the area. Until that railway has been overhauled or rebuilt, you can be sure, Mr. Speaker, that those who travel over it for the 13 hours it takes to cover the distance from Montreal to Chicoutimi are people who have no choice but to do so. However, for the past decade, a modem highway has linked us to Quebec city by a 2J hour drive. This road, which is open the year round, even in the dead of winter, is one of the most attractive highways in Canada, and at each turn reveals new vistas of unsuspected beauty and grandeur. So far, it has been used chiefly by highway transport operators in competing with our railway, for this area has not been ready to accommodate tourists who, on reaching Quebec city, look for interesting side trips they can make.
Hotel organization is therefore a compelling necessity in our district, and that is why I fully support the resolution introduced by my hon. friend from Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken). This resolution is based on a remarkable realism, because it would help reduce


considerably the commercial deficit of Canada towards the United States, while developing most districts of our country.
I know that, in principle, the federal government must not interfere with private business, but every rule has its exceptions and, with regard to the urgent situation prevailing in several districts of the country, in so far as tourism is concerned, some legislation is imperative to remedy the situation. Tourist establishments are in the same position as any small industry unable to borrow from credit organizations or on the money market. The previous administration had partially dealt with small and medium industries in establishing the Industrial Development Bank. The present government would complete the cycle and would break the vicious circle in introducing some legislation allowing the Industrial Development Bank to finance tourist establishments.
Another good way of killing two birds with one stone-that is to say develop the tourist business and at the same time increase revenue for the Canadian National Railways- would be to build several other large hotels in various key areas of the country, and especially in Chicoutimi, where such an establishment has long been a crying need.
This summer, about 10 conventions, provincial and even national in scope, will take place in Chicoutimi; and we always find it very hard to provide the necessary accommodation for all our visitors. Besides, many organizations that would like to come and enjoy our marvelous climate in summer, our unique landscapes and, above all, our proverbial hospitality, have to be turned down through lack of accommodation.
Mr. Speaker, in closing my brief remarks, I repeat that the government should do all it can to offset our unfavourable trade balance with the United States. This resolution provides an excellent means to do so, and it is our duty to support it, so that Canada may regain the rank it has lost in favour of Mexico, as the country most frequently visited by American tourists.

Mr. Speaker, I believe this is the first opportunity this house has had for a full scale debate on the important subject of the tourist industry in Canada and I would therefore congratulate the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) for making it possible to have such a debate under the

resolution now before us. It is rather remarkable that we do not hear more in this chamber about tourism. I have been listening to the contributions made so far in the discussions and it is obvious that the tourist industry in Canada is assuming very substantial proportions.
As we have heard from several speakers, in terms of revenue this industry is surpassed only by the wheat industry and the newsprint industry and I think it is time that we in this chamber began to take a more detailed interest in what is involved in its thriving and growing activity. The whole subject of the increase in tourism, of course, arises from the increasing mobility of the people during the last few decades. Our society has been moving in the direction of shorter hours of work with correspondingly longer hours of leisure. The advent of the automobile and suitable roads to accommodate automobiles have made it possible for almost every citizen on this continent to become mobile. Holidays are now a universal pattern and when all these things are taken into consideration they account for the tremendous upsurge in the tourist industry and the incidental development in those important bi-products-trade and industrial activity.
We have heard from members from the maritimes and from the central parts of Canada and I would now like to relate some of the issues they have raised and some of the suggestions they have made in their discussions to our situation in the province of Manitoba. Manitoba is popularly known as the keystone province because of its geographical position, right in the centre of the federation and has become increasingly popular as a mecca for tourists. The geographical position of Manitoba is partly responsible for this because we are also close to the geographical centre of the North American continent and when I say we I mean particularly my own constituency of Brandon-Souris.
Relating the phrase "the keystone province" to broader issues, I have for the past few years been maintaining that this term not only applies to economic things but that it applies also to the political situation in Canada. We have been in a cross current of opinions from both east and west over the years, and as long ago as 1951 I was making the prophecy that as goes Manitoba so goes the rest of Canada. That has certainly been revealed in the political developments which have taken place within the past few months right across the nation. 1 think the same interpretation would result from an analysis of the developments which have taken place in
28, 1958
Loans to Tourist Resort Operators trade and industry in Manitoba, and certainly it could be used to describe the developing situation in relation to the tourist industry.
It is somewhat significant, I think, to recall that the city of Brandon in the southwestern part of the province of Manitoba was originally known as the wheat city of the west. It has long since lost that title to the province of Saskatchewan but I will suggest this afternoon-and present some facts that will substantiate this suggestion-that as the city of Brandon was once known as the wheat city of the west, the area surrounding it is gradually becoming known as a tourist centre, at least of the continental prairie section of Canada.
I say this because we have a highway passing through this area of the province which is rapidly becoming known as the main street of the Americas. It is a highway which extends from South America through Mexico, right up through the United States, into Canada and on to the northern reaches of Manitoba. At the present time the road terminates in Flin Flon, but with the rapid developments which are taking place in our northern mining communities in Manitoba it will only be a matter of a few years before we have an all-season driveway right through to the port of Churchill.
Along that highway are located some of the most attractive tourist areas not only in Manitoba but in the whole of Canada. I am hoping that at some time those who are interested in the tourist industry in Canada- those responsible for the mass media of information; the press, radio, television, films and other media of that kind-will have their attention attracted to this area. Indeed, I hope that this debate today and this particular presentation may be the means whereby their attention will be directed to this area and that they may do a story on the significance of this main street of the Americas. I propose to deal only with the attractions on the Canadian side, of course.
Right at the border on No. 10 highway we have the international peace garden. Hon. members who have been in this chamber for the past few years will recall that I have had occasion to refer to the international peace garden on former occasions. My interest in the development of this tourist area- because it is that, in addition to being much more than a tourist attraction-began long before I came to the House of Commons. My predecessor in the House of Commons, the late J. E. Matthews, was also vitally interested in its potentialities. The peace garden is a joint Canadian-American project on the Manitoba-North Dakota boundary which is

Loans to Tourist Resort Operators dedicated to the symbolization of the universal desire of the human family for peace. I attended the ceremonies at the opening of the garden back in 1932.
It is a spontaneous project originally sponsored by the international gardeners association-I believe that is the name. They had been searching right along the boundary of Canada for a natural area, an area untouched by the handiwork of man, which might prove a suitable location for a project of this kind. Mr. Moore of Islington, along with other representatives of the international gardeners association, visited the area, and immediately saw its natural advantages. That was in the year 1929. In 1932 the official opening took place with the unveiling of a cairn which had been raised from the native stone of the area. The inscription on this cairn conveyed the purpose of the international peace garden in the following words:
To God in His glory
We two nations dedicate this garden and pledge ourselves that as long as men shall live, we will not take up arms against one another.
That is the purpose of the peace garden, as is simply stated in the words on the cairn. I had to become active in the house in behalf of this project because shortly after I came to the House of Commons an annual federal grant of some $15,000 was suddenly removed and we had to take action regarding the restoration of that grant which was one of the important financial measures by which the garden was being developed. The grant was restored after one year, but at a reduced amount of $10,000. I am delighted to see from the supplementary estimates that this grant is to be increased to the original amount of $15,000, and I must congratulate the government and particularly the minister of northern affairs (Mr. Hamilton) on having taken this action. It demonstrates that both the minister and the government are aware of the growing importance of the tourist industry generally.
I could spend some time discussing this particular aspect of the tourist industry in Manitoba, but I must not yield to that temptation other than to say that in recent years it is encouraging to note that as result of growing publicity thousands of people annually are coming from all parts of North America and indeed from many European countries to hold international gatherings of various kinds in the garden. Others merely come to the garden and try to capture the inspiration which motivated the founders to establish it and dedicate it to the pursuit of peace. I have already indicated that this project is more than simply an aspect of the tourist industry.

We have, for example, an annual meeting of students. Students from both Canada and the United States gather there for discussions of international affairs. I should give honour where honour is due and say that the junior member for Queens (Mr. Mac-quarrie was one of the founding spirits of this international conference. Various service clubs and international bodies are also holding their gatherings there. As a matter of fact, if the necessary facilities were available this would be an ideal place in which to hold a summit meeting. The summit is not very high, of course, because although this is on top of Turtle mountain hon. members will realize that with regard to mountains Manitoba can hardly be compared with British Columbia. But the location, and the spirit behind this garden would, I think, create a very fine atmosphere in which the leaders of the nations of the world could confer.
I must mention this point before proceeding with my remarks. A most interesting development has occurred in recent years. I refer to the establishment of an international music camp in the international peace garden. The founder, as one might guess from his name, is a Minnesota Norwegian, Dr. Merton Utgaard, a well-known professor of music from Northern Illinois university. He first got the idea when working in a C.C.C. camp in the depression of the thirties, on the United States side of the garden. During the first week of July musicians from all parts of Canada and the United States including 500 students of music gathered together at this point. The group included such eminent musicians as the leader of the Winnipeg symphony orchestra. The idea behind it is to have not only a workshop for high school musicians but to eventually send these musicians to various parts of the North American continent and to Europe with a view to contributing to the promotion of peace and international good will and understanding through the medium of music the universal language of the soul. That is the animating purpose behind the meeting of the musicians in the international peace gardens.
There is one handicap in the operation of activity of this kind and that is the lack of suitable buildings and facilities. That is a subject I want to direct to the attention of this government. They will be called upon for assistance as concrete proposals of this kind are formulated. That is just the beginning of the main street of the Americas. Extending right up to the northern part of Manitoba we have a series of tourist attractions. All of these demonstrate the tremendous potentiality of this area, the keystone province, as a source of tourist interest.

I should also mention that our neighbouring state, North Dakota, is so enthusiastic about the peace garden to which I have referred that the licence plates for automobiles issued in that state bear the designation, "The Peace Garden State".
Along the main street of the Americas in Manitoba we have such well-known tourist attractions as lake Killarney, as beautiful as its namesake, Pelican lake and Oak lake. Passing through the city of Brandon, whose virtues I need not extol, we are contemplating there in the immediate future construction of lake Brandon which will add to the value of that area as a tourist centre. Next we come to lake Minnedosa in the constituency of my colleague the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk) and Manitoba national park on Clear lake, one of the finest national parks in our whole system. It is second only to the well-known park at Banff in the number of visitors it attracts annually. This weekend I might add the national park in Manitoba has been celebrating the observance of its 25th anniversary. We then continue on to lake Dauphin, to Flin Flon with its many tourist attractions and then come to the north which is a subject in itself.
All throughout this area there is a great need for development along the lines contained in the proposed resolution of the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. I am grateful that he has provided an opportunity for making some observations in this respect. The problem has been raised by several hon. members concerning just how far private activity should go and to what extent government activity should mingle in this kind of development but that is something that can be sorted out only with experience. The government has already made a large contribution to promoting our tourist industry through the government travel bureau. I believe the publicity that is now being undertaken will assist tremendously in overcoming some of the handicaps that have been mentioned about Canadians going to the United States or even to Europe instead of seeing Canada first. I agree with hon. gentlemen who said we certainly have not been getting the proportion of tourists from that great country to the south of us that we could have expected were the advantages of touring in Canada fully known. The problems of publicity and the provision of adequate hospitality and facilities need solving.
I should make one observation in this regard in which governments should be extremely interested, and that is that the state of our highways in certain areas of Canada leave much to be desired. We know that the roads on the prairies in particular 57071-3-176

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not thought I would be following directly another Manitoba member in this debate. Perhaps it is a good thing for by strength of numbers and conclusiveness of argument we may be able to convince members of the house to visit and enjoy our fair province.
With regard to the resolution before us, as many of the previous speakers have pointed out the Canadian tourist association is a nonprofit organization serving the Canadian tourist industry and as the national voice of Canada's tourist industry it represents almost every phase of the Canadian economy. It has been further pointed out by previous speakers that the tourist industry in Canada is an extensive business and that part of everyone's income comes from visitors to our communities and to the country. It has been said that tourism means much to Canada and I agree completely with that statement. However, apart from the national picture as a whole I should like to point out to the house that the tourist trade in the province of Manitoba is an important segment of the national tourist business and, in effect, has been growing larger and larger every year.
Many people across the country do not realize that the city of Winnipeg is located only 60 miles from the United States border and Manitoba as the keystone province in its favourable geographical position and with its abundance of tourist attractions now occupies an important status in the Canadian tourist business. You have heard my good friend,

Loans to Tourist Resort Operators the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), extol the virtues of the tourist attractions in his constituency and the area surrounding it in the southwest portion of the province. I do not intend to repeat his remarks but rather I should like to discuss the tourist business in the province of Manitoba as a whole with, of course, some reference to the city of Winnipeg.
In 1957 more visitors came to our province and spent more money than in any previous year. The estimated value for 1957 is well over $31 million and it is considered that this amount was spent by at least one million tourists. For the year 1957 the province of Manitoba had the largest percentage increase in the tourist industry of any province in Canada. Another significant index of the upward trend in Manitoba's tourist volume is that for the first six months of 1958 there was an increase of 12.9 per cent over the corresponding months of 1957 in the number of foreign vehicles coming into the province. This is the largest increase of any province in Canada, with our closest competitor being the province of British Columbia. Present indications suggest that the year 1958 will be the best tourist year in the history of the province. The current period of economic adjustment in capital investment, industrial activity and consumer purchases appears to have had little, if any, reflection on the tourist trade of Manitoba.
It is noted that families and sportsmen are already allocating more money for travel and holidays than ever before. Disposable income available for travel and vacations has increased more than most commodity prices and service charges. The factor of money is not alone in influencing the tourist trade in Manitoba. As is pointed out in the Manitoba tourist industry report, a publication of the department of industry and commerce of the province of Manitoba, "time itself is a big factor".
In the states of the United States closest to our province paid vacations for hourly workers have more than doubled since 1939. Today well over 95 per cent of hourly workers have vacations with pay. Four times as many companies now allow three weeks vacation as did ten years ago. The five-day week has become standard practice throughout business and industry. Thus all facets of the tourist trade, theoretically at least, have a stake in over 120 days of an employee's year. This figure is made up of the annual vacation plus statutory holidays and week ends.
The trend in Manitoba this year is reflecting the influence of these factors. Capital investments in new motels, hotels, resorts, hunting


and fishing lodges, in additions and modernizations to be completed in 1958, will see the greatest amount of investment in tourist facilities ever made in a single year in this province. This in itself is reason enough for me to give serious consideration to the resolution before the house tonight.
The population of our province is approximately 850,000 with roughly half of this number being concentrated in the Winnipeg area. From the Winnipeg of 1874 with 4,000 people to the present Winnipeg with close to half a million people, Winnipeg's growth has been truly amazing. Today greater Winnipeg, which includes Winnipeg proper and its twin city of St. Boniface across the Red river, stands as Canada's fourth largest city and the leading industrial and agricultural centre of three provinces. Every year, and this is a point I should like to emphasize, the city is host to more than 600,000 tourists and, whatever the purpose of their visit, you may rest assured that Winnipeg offers them a warm hearted welcome. The mayor of the city of Winnipeg would, I think, agree with me in saying that the key to our city in effect is available at all times for all visitors to the capital city of the province of Manitoba.
The fact that a great deal more than half of the estimated number of tourists who come into the province of Manitoba visit the city of Winnipeg is also another reason why I, as the member for one of the Winnipeg constituencies, should consider seriously this resolution. The city of Winnipeg welcomes the tourist trade for the city can provide adequate accommodation, is a mecca for visiting shoppers and has within the limits of greater Winnipeg over 1,000 green acres of park made up in the main of spacious Kildonan, St. Vital and Assiniboine parks which I am sure you would all enjoy.
Throughout the year the city of Winnipeg has a wide selection of entertainment ranging from sports as played in our magnificent new arena and stadium by professional hockey, baseball and football teams, namely the Warriors, the Goldeyes and, of course, our famous Blue Bombers,-I may say that Winnipeg is one of the few cities in Canada that is able to support three professional athletic teams-to the new modern Assiniboine Downs race track and, on the more cultural side, the Royal Winnipeg ballet and the outdoor Rainbow Stage at Kildonan park to the latest production at the Playhouse theatre. Of course, the tourist's visit would not be complete unless it included the colour and pageantry of the very interesting and beautiful festivals of the various ethnic groups in our fair city. Whatever the tourist's taste may be, he may rest assured that in the city of Winnipeg he will not be bored.

In concluding this brief resume of the attractions of the city of Winnipeg and the province of Manitoba,-I must admit it is very brief and I could go on for many hours but I have not got that many hours-I should like now to dwell on the resolution with regard to the financial aspects. I have attempted to show the house that we have a tourist industry in our province which is very important to the people of Manitoba. This makes it necessary that I consider this resolution in all its details. Who benefits from the tourist trade? In the first place it should be established that what is called the tourist trade is, in fact, a combination of many private businesses and government services. In most cases, they work independently, but all contribute goods or services which are used or consumed by the tourist.
Whatever one may do for a living, whether it is in industry, farming, the wholesale or retail trade, or some other business or profession, part of your income is derived from the visitors to your community or to our country. The Manitoba government has done a great deal of research on the tourist industry. I should like to take up some of your time by quoting from figures which show a breakdown of every tourist dollar spent in our province. It is estimated that the retail stores all over the province are the chief beneficiary of the tourist spending, in that 31 cents of every tourist dollar is spent in retail outlets. About 24 cents goes for accommodation of one kind or another in hotels, modern hunting and fishing lodges, camp grounds and trailer parks. Restaurants, dining rooms and snack bars collect 21 cents of every tourist dollar. With regard to this last factor, the province of Manitoba estimates that in 1957-how they procured this estimate, I do not know-the consumption of foodstuffs by tourists amounted to 600,000 eggs; 2.5 million pounds of grain products; 1.5 millions pounds of sugar and syrup; 725,000 pounds of butter; 7.5 million pints of milk and 4.5 million pounds of meat and meat products. These figures aptly demonstrate the large and important tourist industry in the province of Manitoba.
Of every tourist dollar spent in our province, there was 15 cents spent for gas and oil. Altogether, in 1957, tourists purchased $5.5 million worth of gas and oil. You can just imagine, on the gasoline tax alone the treasury of the province of Manitoba collected about half a million dollars. I was amazed when I was in receipt of these figures to find that the tourist industry of Manitoba actually was so large. Of the balance of the tourist's dollar, 9 cents was used for entertainment and miscellaneous unclassified 57071-3-176J
Loans to Tourist Resort Operators purchases. From these official figures, it may be seen that the tourist trade benefits many different sections of our economy in Manitoba and, of course, across Canada as a nation.
Conversely, the introduction of these important tourist dollars means a high standard of living for many of our people. It is reasonable to assume that the tourist industry will play an increasingly important role in the future in broadening the base of our economy. We may make this reasonable assumption, and I make it in all seriousness, because of definite trends in high and rising incomes; the allocation of more consumer dollars for vacation and travel; the increase in the number of privately owned automobiles; the growing participation in outdoor activities by both sportsmen and family groups. Of course, so far as Manitoba is concerned, there is the further fact that there is close proximity of a receptive class of prospects for travelling and holidaying in our province. Because of the importance of the tourist industry and the reasonable assumption that it will play an increasingly important role in the future, we are well advised to study this resolution with regard to long term financing for tourist resort operators.
As the brief submitted by the Canadian tourist association to the government concerning a tourist establishment improvement loan act-which is much the same thing as this resolution proposes-points out, the tourist industry is composed mainly of small businesses. While there are some larger establishments, the greater percentage of restaurants and accommodation establishments are small. Many are, in fact, family enterprises. The brief goes on to point out that one of the major deterrents to improvement of tourist facilities is the lack of credit resources. The brief suggests that the tourist industry needs long term credit at reasonable rates of interest. With this suggestion, I am in complete accord.
However, with regard to a long term credit plan, I would point out that it would be preferable for this house to consider at just what point within the tourist industry as a whole, such credit plan would be needed. I have pointed out previously that in the province of Manitoba, the largest portion of the tourist dollar, 31 cents, is spent in retail stores. Surely, if any long term financing plan is needed for the tourist industry, it is most appropriate to consider the extension of such a plan to the independent retail merchant. Even before I was elected to office I had given a great deal of thought to the importance to our economy of the small retail merchant. There are many reasons for my interest in this field, but probably the main

Loans to Tourist Resort Operators influencing factor was that my father had his own retail business in the city of Winnipeg for a great many years. It was only natural that I became aware of his problems, and consequently the problems of the independent retail merchant in Winnipeg today.
As I have pointed out, the greater portion of the tourist dollar is spent in retail outlets. Therefore, I should like to consider this resolution as it affects retail outlets in the city of Winnipeg. It has been forecast that by this time next year there will be an additional $20 million investment in supermarkets operating in the city of Winnipeg. I have no quarrel with this, for the supermarket idea is beneficial to the housewife and to the community at large. This development shows an extreme faith in the future of the city of Winnipeg and the province of Manitoba. To emphasize the extent of this investment, I should like to read from part of an editorial in the Winnipeg Tribune of Thursday, July 24:
The $20 million investment planned here in the next year-

I could perhaps go further at this point and dwell on the great needs of small business and industry in Canada today, for some kind of long term financing is drastically needed. This question has been discussed in this house on other occasions. The government is especially aware of this problem and is busy at the present moment setting up a small business section to consider these difficulties with a view to finding some solution.
As the Canadian tourist association stated in its brief, it welcomes the expressed intention of the government to take measures to alleviate the difficulties which operators of small enterprises encounter for the improvement and expansion of business. In any event, I heartily approve of this resolution. The hon. member who proposed it is to be commended for bringing it to the attention of the house. However, I should certainly like to see the resolution broadened to bring in the independent retail merchants and other small business and industry throughout Canada. As I have already pointed out, the tourist in Manitoba spends the greater part of his dollar in the retail outlets, and I believe any consideration that might be given to the tourist resort operators with regard to long term financing and credit should be given to the independent retail merchants across this country.
This subject of long term financing, of course, is something that deserves diligent and careful scrutiny and study in order that some constructive suggestion could be offered to the tourist industry and small business right across this country. If I may do so at this point, I should like to say that I have been in the house all day and have been greatly interested in the remarks of the

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR JOINT LOANS TO TOURIST RESORT OPERATORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate which has been going on here today is as good evidence as you could find of the growing awareness there is in the country of the value of the tourist industry as it is and as it can be. The resolution submitted by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) is also an indication of the awareness of the necessity for the development of our facilities if we are to maintain the position that we now hold and certainly if we are to improve that situation in the country.
In recent years the tourist industry has become one of our major industries. It is an industry with a tremendous potential; but that potential will be realized only if the facilities to cater to the tourist trade are provided. As has been pointed out here today in many of the speeches, the tourist industry is largely in the hands of the independent or small businessman whose financial resources are limited and who, owing to a relatively short season, is unable to secure from the operations of his business the additional capital that is required for capital expenditures. Consequently, if the very people who will provide the means of expanding our tourist industry are going to be able to do so, they must have access to the money they require.
The resolution suggests that the federal government can make this money available through a system of extending credit. There has been a suggestion-and I think it is a reasonable one-that it is perhaps not entirely the responsibility of government to make this money available, that there are other channels or other sources by means of which funds could be made available to the tourist industry. I feel that we must not lose sight of the fact that the government has not unlimited credit and cannot meet every requirement of business and industry in Canada. Nevertheless, if there is in any industry a branch capable of a development that will return to government more than the cost of creating the necessary development in the industry, then probably there is a good case for federal government participation.
In that case I am inclined to disagree with the hon. member for Port Arthur who suggested that those who support this resolution
2790	HOUSE OF
Loans to Tourist Resort Operators are endorsing socialism because by making credit facilities available and by loaning money secured as to repayment plus interest the government would not be giving anything away. It would simply be providing a facility which in its turn will ensure repayment with interest of these loans and this is something which is not necessarily true of socialist ventures.
There are in Canada many areas where there is a highly developed tourist industry including regions which are internationally as well as nationally famed for their beauty and recreational attractions which are perhaps developed as far as is possible. There are other areas which are only now becoming appreciated and it is only recently that people have realized what such areas have to offer to the tourist industry. These regions are being opened by the development of our highway system; the trans-Canada highway alone has provided access to regions which will I imagine in the years to come constitute some of the major tourist areas in Canada. This will only be so, however, if cash advances are available to people who wish to go into the areas and provide the facilities which must be provided. Many such regions are now virtually wilderness without even a gas pump. Everything will have to start from the bare ground and be built up.
A tremendous amount of capital investment will be necessary and, as has been pointed out during the course of this debate, such capital is not at present available to the small operator at a reasonable rate of interest or for a sufficiently lengthy period. Many of these areas are areas which produce primary products only, in most cases supporting only seasonal industries. They cannot support a secondary industry and consequently have but one source of revenue. In order to develop they will of course require further sources of revenue but it may be years before they can be developed to this point. With no factories or like facilities the people who live in such areas have inadequate income at this time but there is one point in their favour and that is that in many places their natural attractions give them a potentiality for development as popular tourist resorts.
The lack of year round industrial payrolls is of course a serious disadvantage but such sources of revenue might be provided by the development of the tourist industry which in turn would provide the funds required to create the necessary facilities with which to satisfy the travelling public. The whole potential of the tourist industry in Canada can be related to these areas which are only now


beginning to be viewed with an understanding of what can be done by the careful expenditure of money and with adequate advertising. Such regions are not sufficiently prosperous to maintain a reasonable standard of living.
For instance, to particularize, there are regions in this country which are primarily farming areas growing seasonal crops and providing employment for perhaps six or eight months a year-some of them even less than that. There is an idea which has started to grow in recent years and which is not a new one-it is perhaps a very old idea but like so many old ideas is now being reconsidered with a fresh approach-that is the development of the farm vacation. No one will argue that in this country there does not exist the need for improving the level of farm incomes and any measure which could increase the income of our farm people will not only be of direct benefit to them but it will also be of benefit to the country as a whole. The farm vacation is only now beginning to be appreciated although that appreciation is limited to some extent to eastern Canada. It is, however, an idea which could spread although there are few farmers who have the necessary additional revenue required to create facilities necessary to cope with the tourist trade.
The idea of a farm vacation sounds very good and I have encountered people who have considered the idea and some have actually begun to develop their farms to provide such vacations. However, when they find out what is necessary in the way of accommodation and in order to meet the provincial health regulations and the demands of the modern travelling public they realize that the farm vacation today is not the same as it was 25 or 30 years ago. Farm incomes are not adequate to provide the facilities which people have come to expect and the farmers have sufficient difficulty in finding the capital they require to cover their ordinary expenditures so that if they are to develop the tourist trade they must have access to additional revenue on a long term basis and at reasonable rates of interest.
A further problem in Canada is the problem of providing employment during winter months. We have heard during the course of the debate that the tourist industry is in many cases a seasonal one, generally speaking, for perhaps four to five months of the year. The largest proportion of our tourist business is done during the summer months but there is no reason why we could not extend our facilities to include more highly

developed winter vacation programs thus providing a valuable source of winter employment. We have the climatic conditions necessary for every type of winter recreation. The Canadian people are in the habit of taking their holidays in the summer months because it is then that facilities are available to them and except in a relatively small part of the country little is done to provide facilities for winter vacations or recreation. There is at present very little encouragement for Canadians as a whole to take winter holidays and much should be done to provide the accommodation so that such vacations could be promoted.
Skiing facilities, sleighing facilities, ice for skating and all the other winter recreations that build up into a typical winter resort town are expensive, and the accommodation which will serve them is expensive. The cost of heating has to be very carefully considered; it has to be done on the most economical basis, and that usually means an expensive type of installation.
There are many regions which are multiple regions for recreation, and if these regions can be helped to extend their season and increase their opportunity for earning income by providing facilities that operate more nearly on a 12 months a year basis then we will have further strengthened the economy of many regions in Canada which now have only a limited or restricted economic basis, regions which will never realize their potential unless some means is found of establishing their economy on a 12 month year.
There is a further benefit. If Canadians find that winter recreational facilities are available to them, we can expect that more and more people will, over a period of time, choose to take winter vacations instead of jamming the greater proportion of Canadian vacations into the summer months, which in turn will mean that important employment opportunities in the winter will be available, at least on a temporary basis, to many thousands of people who will supply the places vacant in our factories, businesses and so on to replace vacationing employees. We will find out also that as we are not only interested in providing recreational opportunities for our own people but also for the benefit of foreign tourists, particularly for those people in the United States who come to Canada in search of something different, I am sure that just as Canadians head south for a winter in the sun, United States citizens would find considerable pleasure in the novelty of a winter in the north. But until we provide the kind of
Loans to Tourist Resort Operators accommodation which they expect and which they are accustomed to finding at home, we will never get them.
It comes back to this; that if we are to realize our potential and if we are to develop this industry which is of proven value to the country we must find the means of aiding financially those who are engaged in the business and who want to grow in the business. The government can provide some of the necessary assistance through a program such as is suggested in this resolution. It is to be hoped that the provinces, realizing the value of the industry, will undertake similar programs. I would also express the hope that our regular channels of finance-the banks, the mortgage companies and financial houses-will take a fresh look at the tourist industry in Canada and realize that though at the present time it operates on a season of four or five months, with the proper kind of encouragement, capital addition and development the industry could function during a far longer season. The season could be at least doubled in many areas.
But this will never occur as long as we approach the problem timidly or without imagination. Therefore I feel that we in this house must consider this resolution with imagination and certainly not with timidity, and I hope the government will realize that there is a tremendous opportunity here, and that much can be done. Although there are limitations on the amount of money which the government can make available to any one sector of the economy, there is reason to believe that whatever is spent in this field will be returned to the coffers of the government many times over.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, inasmuch as the tourist industry is a very important one in my riding, I am very pleased to support the resolution which has been proposed today by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken).
In doing so I will abide by your observations, sir, and a proper interpretation of the rules of the house, and not speak at any length on the many beauties of my riding and the many attractions which are offered to tourists and travellers. However, I should like to say in passing without covering all my riding that the areas bordering the Trent canal, Presqu'ile provincial park and the district around Rice lake offer almost anything in the way of a tourist attraction that can be asked for by any vacationer.
The resolution which has been proposed asks for government assistance to tourist operators by way of loans for capital improvement, and I feel sure that any hon. member
2792	HOUSE OF
Loans to Tourist Resort Operators who has a segment of the tourist industry in his riding will have been made aware of the difficulties of tourist operators in obtaining loans where necessary for improvement or an extension to their establishments. Long term loans, which seem to be the most necessary, are the ones most difficult to obtain. The banks seem to be reluctant to lend money to these people on a long term basis, although the fact that the industry has managed to survive for so long should be an argument in favour of loans being made available. I think a good case can be made out for the tourist industry in Canada and I should like to cover some of the points which I think support this contention.
The tourist industry in Canada has become the third largest industry. Probably not many of us realize that this is the situation, but over the years the industry has grown slowly and without much publicity until it has reached its present dimensions. The industry is national in scope. It extends from coast to coast, and every segment of the Canadian economy benefits from its achievements. Today, every one travels and takes vacations. In the past it was not possible for everyone to travel or take a vacation and this was perhaps a luxury of the well-to-do. In this day, however, vacations and travel are not restricted to one class of people but are taken advantage of by everyone.
Tourism is promoting trade for Canada and in assisting tourism we can help overcome the trade deficit which we have with the United States at the present time and which has been causing us so much concern.
I have in my hand a copy of a pamphlet published by the Canadian tourist association from which I should like to quote concerning Canada's present status in the tourist trade with the United States:
Canada used to get the largest share of the money which United States residents spent visiting other countries, but that is no longer the case. Since 1953, Europe has attracted many more United States visitor dollars than Canada, even without counting the cost of transportation.
Indeed, spending by United States travellers in all countries outside the United States has almost doubled since 1949. But during the same period, United States spending in Canada increased by only 23 per cent.
Canada's overseas competitors for tourists have not only captured the increased business that we might have had, they have quadrupled their share of travel expenditures made by Canadians themselves.
Spending by Canadians abroad has reached such a point that Canadians travelling in the United States and other countries took more than one-half billion dollars out of Canada, in 1957.
I believe a good case can be made out for promoting the Canadian tourist industry and therefore helping to overcome our adverse trade balance. Also, tourism is a means of


promoting national unity, a means by which Canadians can get to know Canada better. I feel the Canadian people should be encouraged to travel across their country and to see the many beauty spots that can be found here at home.
Another feature of the tourist industry is that tourist income as an addition to the wealth of this country takes little if anything from our natural resources. The services which are provided by the tourist industry do not involve any costs for transportation. As I see it, the task of the tourist industry in Canada is twofold. In the first place, the industry wants to persuade Canadians to vacation in Canada and, in the second place, it wants to persuade others to vacation here. To my mind these objectives can be accomplished in two ways. The first is by advertising and the second is by providing enough of the best possible facilities for tourists.
In order to accomplish the latter objective capital is required for improvements and expansion. I am not going to go into any detail about the improvements that are required but certainly we all know that over the years tourist establishments have come to offer a great deal more by way of comfort and convenience than they did, let us say, 20 or 30 years ago. Providing this capital for improvements is an area in which the government can assist to promote the tourist industry of Canada.
Most of the governments at all levels in Canada at the present time are spending a great deal of money in advertising and attracting tourists to our country. It seems to me that money could be made to do even more than it does now by ensuring that no one in this country who is desirous of improving his establishment is unable to do so because of a lack of a source from which to borrow funds. If we place anyone who is desirous of improving his establishment in a position to borrow funds, in that way we are spending good money after good money.
In other countries assistance is given to tourist establishments. In the United States, for instance, under the small business administration provisions a hotel or resort operator can borrow up to $250,000 for renovating or refurnishing for a ten-year term at an interest rate of 5 or 6 per cent depending on the particular application. The United States has also made money available through the export-import bank for the developing of hotels and accommodation in foreign countries. Other countries including Belgium, Ireland, Norway, Great Britain and Switzerland give assistance to their tourist operators by way of various plans. The economic progress of a country is measured

by the impression that is made on the visitors to that country. In my view that impression is made in the places where the visitors stay when they are visiting the country. I am sure we all want to give a good impression of Canada to those who visit this country so they will return with their friends and have the faith in Canada we want them to have.
Having attempted to make out a case for the tourist industry and for the provision of loans to that industry by the government, let us consider just how this assistance might be given. In the first place it could be given by way of a government guaranteed loan similar to those available under the National Housing Act. Secondly, it could be given under the industrial development bank. The industrial development bank which was established in 1944 makes available loans to industrial enterprises. The preamble of the act which incorporated the industrial development bank reads as follows:
Whereas it is desirable to establish an industrial development bank to promote the economic welfare of Canada by increasing the effectiveness of monetary action through ensuring the availability of credit to industrial enterprises which may reasonably be expected to prove successful if a high level of national income and employment is maintained, by supplementing the activities of other lenders and by providing capital assistance to industry with particular consideration to the financing problems of small enterprises-
Tourist operators do not come within the ambit or scope of this act at the present time but it seems to me that if the spirit and wording of this preamble are to be carried to their logical conclusion tourist operators could well be included within the ambit of this legislation. The interpretation section of the act defines industrial enterprise as follows:
2 (d) "industrial enterprise" means a business in which the manufacture, processing or refrigeration of goods, wares and merchandise or the building, alteration or repair of ships or vessels or the generating or distributing of electricity is carried on;-
That was the definition in 1944. In 1956 the definition was extended to take in even more business enterprises. I believe that this statute could be further extended to give some form of loan to our tourist industry and tourist operators. I hope the day is forthcoming when there will be set up in this country a small business agency in government to provide small business liaison with government and advice on assistance measures as announced and outlined in the speech from the throne. Possibly something will be forthcoming when that takes place. I think the measure proposed by the resolution could not help but be of benefit to the country. Benefiting the tourist industry, it is bound to benefit the country as a whole. Therefore
Loans to Tourist Resort Operators I am very pleased to offer my support for the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take part in the debate and perhaps attack the problem from a little different angle. I think that the motion proposed by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) is very good but in my view it does not go far enough. Because tourism is such a great industry in Canada and can become much greater I think we have to do perhaps a little more than the resolution proposes.
To me the industry has four basic components. First of all, there is the basic resource, your beauty, your recreational facility, your developed resource. Second, there is the problem of transportation because no beautiful spot is of any value whatsoever if people cannot get there to look at it. I feel that the third component of the industry is advertising because again if people do not know the beauty is there they are not likely to go to see it. The fourth and primary component is accommodation of the tourist once he gets here, which is what we have been discussing. I submit that any one of the four can have some effect upon the capital required, the type of capital required and the length of time it may be required. Therefore I feel it would be of advantage to have a look at these four basic requirements to see if we can come up with any answers after we do so.
The first one is the basic resource. We in Canada are richly endowed. We have magnificent scenery from coast to coast, some of which has been set aside by previous governments in the form of national parks. I should like to say something about them later. Certainly we have an abundance of beautiful scenery from British Columbia to Newfoundland, anywhere you want to go. We also have an abundance of natural recreational facilities for fishing, hunting and skiing in every province of Canada. Then there are our developed resources of which we have a great many in Canada. We are in the process of finishing one of the greatest, the St. Lawrence seaway, and we are just starting on another, the South Saskatchewan dam. These will be great tourist attractions in the years to come and must be taken into consideration in any discussion of the Canadian tourist industry.
Other developed resources which we have and need more of are those developed for recreation. We need more and better golf courses right across the country. We need more and better fish hatcheries so that we can stock some of our depleted lakes. Then

In nearly every community there is some resource and all that needs to be done is to advertise it and let other people know you have it. The people of Jasper-Edson feel we have been fairly well advertised by the presence of Jasper national park and we have a particular interest in the tourist industry.
The next natural component of the tourist industry which we should discuss is highways and means of transportation to our beauty spots and recreational facilities. I think highways are the most essential accommodation required for our tourists. We have to provide them with decent highways on which to travel. In that regard I should like to suggest that in my part of the country we are waiting anxiously for the completion of the Yellowhead highway. It will be the greatest boon to the tourist industry in northern Alberta since the inception of the province.
Looking at highways nationally, we are nearing the completion of our first trans-Canada highway. We in the west, especially in the northern part of the prairies, would like to see a start on a second trans-Canada highway. I think these highways are primarily for our tourist industry and not primarily for tourists from outside the country because we are tourists when we go to the next town to see what it is like. It is for this great mass of humanity on wheels that we have to have more and better national highways. That deals with the first two components of the tourist industry.
The third one is advertising. We have been spending a considerable amount of money on advertising but I do not feel we have been spending enough because any good business will tell you that there is a direct relationship between good advertising and the profits which accrue to the business. The more you can advertise the better the results will be. It has already been proven in the tourist industry that by a massive type of advertising the number of tourists going to any one particular area can be greatly increased.
Then we come to the question of accommodation, which is directly covered by the resolution. I support the resolution wholeheartedly, not on a socialistic basis, as the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) has suggested, but rather from the point of view that the government, acting as a catalyst in the tourist industry, can stimulate it and make it grow.
