I should like to mention some of the particular problems tourist resort operators have in the national parks because here we have an additional factor over and above those encountered by tourist resort operators outside the parks. I may say that this is a very important matter because according to the statistics 75 per cent of the close to two million people who visited the province of Alberta in 1956 entered one of the three national parks. Therefore the whole administration of our national parks, the facilities provided and the operation of tourist resorts in the parks become very important. The tourist operators in the parks are at a disadvantage for the reason that they do not hold title to their land. They have leases which may vary anywhere from 10 years to a maximum of 21 years, but certainly you cannot get a long term loan when you only have a 10-year lease. Therefore these people are at a particular disadvantage. Yet they have a special responsibility in providing accommodation in these show places of Canada.
At a later date I should like to see the government tackle the serious problem of national parks administration, particularly with regard to the matter of townsites within our national parks. I feel very strongly that we must face up to the fact that we have to have townsites in these parks and therefore it is high time that we had some policy with regard to them and set up some sort of local government so that the people could have a say in what is going on in their own towns. Right now they do not.
They are probably the only people in Canada who have no local self-government. The park is administered by a superintendent, and the superintendent refers most things to Ottawa. People who have their affairs administered by someone who is
2,000	miles away may become angry very quickly over the suggestions and decisions meted out by mail or telephone. This will be a difficult problem in the development of our parks as tourist resorts, and as these parks are used more and more by people, not only from outside Canada but inside Canada, as the result of improved highways.
In so far as Canadians are concerned, these parks were set aside for our use. We would like to see better highways and better accommodation provided. If I may, for a few moments, go back over these points, I would say that these assets of the tourist industry seem to fall into the four categories to which I have referred. I should like to make the suggestion at this time that in view of the importance of the tourist industry the government should give consideration to the

establishment of a separate ministry to look after that industry. This ministry should have control over our national highways; over our national parks; over our Canadian travel bureau, and should have a branch which would look after not only the financing of these tourist resorts but also the education of operators in operation and maintenance according to certain standards. It would be, of course, through our national parks that the federal government would get jurisdiction in this regard. I feel such a proposal is worthy of study at the moment because, as I say, our national parks and our national highways are basically a part of this tourist industry. Of course, our Canadian travel bureau would fit into such a ministry, as well. I should like to repeat the suggestion to the government that they give consideration to the establisment of a new ministry, a ministry of tourism, which would look after our national parks, our national highways, and so on.
There is one other point I should like to make. I am in agreement with what the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. Fleming) said to the effect that an attempt might be made to make some of our tourist accommodation available on a year-round basis rather than on a seasonal basis. Naturally capital will be needed for such a change because it will cost quite a bit to provide that accommodation. We, in Jasper, are particularly interested in that aspect of the proposal because we have some of the best undeveloped skiing country that there is. We feel that government leadership in this regard would be worth while. I am in agreement with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) with regard to the winter Olympics in 1964. I have no quarrel with the suggestion, but I would suggest that the winter games be split between Banff and Jasper because by 1964 we hope to have our new road between Banff and Jasper open. I should like to urge upon the government once again that they give serious consideration to the immediate construction of the Yellowhead highway through Edmonton, Kamloops, to Vancouver.

Mr. Speaker, at this hour of the evening, after practically a full day of debate on a question such as this, it is rather hard to make remarks that are not repetitious. However, I should like to take this opportunity to commend the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) for introducing a resolution at this time to authorize the making of loans jointly with an approved lending institution to tourist resort operators for the purpose of constructing or making improvements to tourist accommodation.
I feel that this resolution is an extremely important one, first, because it has to do with an industry which, as so many hon. members today have indicated, ranks third in importance in bringing dollars into Canada. In fact, in that respect, I understand it ranks next to newsprint and wheat. Hence it is of great importance to the people of Canada and to our entire economy.
Second, I feel it is important because, in spite of the natural advantages we have in

beautiful rivers and lakes, unexcelled bathing beaches, tremendous mountain ranges and an abundance of good hunting and fishing grounds, the combination of which make for natural tourist attractions all year round; in spite of all these things the tourist industry in Canada has not kept pace with the tourist industry in other countries.
A great many hon. members have extolled the beauty and the attractions to be found in their own ridings. Coming as I do from a riding in western Ontario, perhaps I do not have quite so many natural attractions of which to boast. However, in that connection, I should like to mention the work that has been done by the Grand river conservation commission in providing three lakes which today are attracting a tremendous number of tourists.
Mr. Speaker, there is one thing that it is rather hard to understand in looking back through the records of the last few years. Although the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources has been spending a great deal of money in promoting this industry and expects to spend over $1.5 million in the coming year to advertise Canada through the media of newspapers, radio, television and magazines, it is hard to understand why there has been so little discussion in this house on this important industry. As I have indicated and as has been indicated by others, it ranks next to wheat in importance in bringing dollars into Canada. I do not want to belittle the position of our wheat industry but if half the time that has been taken up in this house in talking about wheat had been spent in talking about the tourist industry probably we would not be in the deficit position in that respect in which we are today.
There must be a reason why we are losing out in this industry, why more people are not coming to Canada and why more of our own people are travelling in other countries. I feel that this resolution gives us an opportunity to examine this entire question so that steps may be taken not only to attract tourists to Canada but to make their stay in Canada more pleasant and happy.
This resolution has to do with the provision of tourist accommodation. As the brief of the Canadian tourist association would indicate, some of our present tourist accommodation is many years old. The people who travel make comparisons; and if the cost is not as fair as it is elsewhere, the surroundings not as pleasant, the food not as tasty or not served in as bright and pleasant surroundings and if. the accommodation lacks all the modern facilities for comfort and convenience, then in spite of our natural attractions the tourist may not return and

will not be an advertising medium through which more people will be attracted to Canada.
As one of the briefs presented would indicate, it is of no use to advertise if we cannot handle the customers. It is of no use to build up our plant if we are not prepared to take adequate steps to keep those customers. There are many media through which the tourist's stay and travel in Canada can be made more pleasant. I sometimes feel that our railroads could do more in helping to hold and to increase this very important industry. Too often we find, as in my part of the country, the railroad facilities taking the tourist to the lovely summer resorts on the shores of lake Huron and Georgian bay are uncomfortable and inadequate. Too often we find on busy week ends, when more people are travelling to these resorts, some of the oldest coaches that were ever made are pressed into service, coaches with hard seats and with no modern air-conditioning facilities, and tourists are compelled to use these coaches at the end of a long and tiresome journey. Certainly these conditions do not improve public relations as far as the tourist industry is concerned. No doubt there are many people who, in spite of the beauty of these resorts and the relaxation to be found there, prefer to go some place else rather than take these arduous train trips.
In the same connection, may I say that I sometimes wonder whether our provincial governments in their road-building programs give proper consideration to the fact that considerable inconvenience is caused to the tourist during the summer vacation period, and the heavy tourist season, by broken-up roads and rough, dusty detours.
Today, as figures indicate, more and more of our people from Canada are travelling abroad rather than investigating and enjoying the wonderful natural beauty that we have in Canada. In travelling abroad they will compare the accommodation provided. Does ours compare favourably with what they will find abroad? Is it as convenient and is it as comfortable? Through this resolution ways and means will be provided so that this accommodation in Canada may be improved and as indicated by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) and the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Thompson) there are indications of what is being done in this connection by means of providing loans in the United States. Many countries in the world appreciate the importance of the tourist industry and Professor L. Dudley Stamp of the London University, London, England, has this to say in a very interesting little bulletin put out by the Canadian tourist association:
Loans to Tourist Resort Operators
Tourism is the most important industry today without any exception whatever. It employs more people and has a larger turn-over of money than any other.
I feel Canada should do something concrete to assist this industry. We are living in a high cost economy; we have money or we have found money for our home builders, our farmers and our industrialists through the medium of government loans and the same principle holds good in respect of the tourist industry where the cost of modern accommodation has gone up by leaps and bounds and it is impossible for the small operator to provide the requirements.
Finally, I would again like to commend the member who, through the medium of this resolution has brought this matter to the attention of the government and I sincerely hope it will receive the consideration it deserves.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak in support of this resolution I would like to say a word or two from the point of view of the travel agent. I do not think I will be called to order for speaking at great length about the tourist attractions of my riding because, although we have some buildings which might be worth seeing, we have not even a post office to show you, a fact which I have mentioned previously in this house. We do have, however, 120,000 people, each one of whom is a potential customer for the tourist operator, which should be of the greatest interest to those concerned.
Much has already been said about the importance of the tourist trade to our economy and if we are to correct the imbalance in this trade as it relates to that of other countries we will have to do everything possible to attract overseas tourists to Canada. To this end the operations of camp, motels, lodges, restaurants and all other establishments catering to the tourist industry must be equipped in order to provide the facilities obtainable in foreign countries. As it would benefit everyone I have no hesitation in supporting the making available of money at the going rate to enable these operators to equip their premises in a suitable manner. One of the immediate effects of lending such funds for this purpose would be that the lenders would be able to exercise some supervision over operations in order to safeguard their interests and the tourist business is a field in which we have been falling down despite the excellent work done by the Canadian tourist association and the various provincial travel departments.

Loans to Tourist Resort Operators
The travel agent constantly receives complaints from his clients about food, facilities, rates and even lack of courtesy in some of our tourist resorts and, as he depends on repeat business for his livelihood, the travel agent is not likely to send clients to places where they will be dissatisfied. At one time a client of mine was telling me about the meal situation in some of our resorts and he made the remark that when you go into some of these places you never know whether you are going to get a burnt offering or a bloody sacrifice. In some cases this is truly indicative of what happens.
It is only recently that in Canada the value of the travel agent has been recognized in the promotion of the tourist trade but we still have a long way to go before the same benefits now accruing to foreign travel as a result of his services will be available to the Canadian travel industry. In Canada there are many tourist resorts which favourably compare with any in the world and many thousands of dollars are spent annually on advertising these resorts through various media. Yet there is very little if any encouragement given to the travel agent by way of information concerning facilities, rates, reservations or commissions. Most of such agents make no charge for their services and depend upon commissions paid by the resort and the carriers in order to operate their businesses. People are now becoming aware of this fact and are going to the travel agent for advice when they consider where to go for their holidays. Needless to say they are being advised to go to places which provide the most profit for their agent and, as pointed out by the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Houck), the commissions paid by carriers for international travel are in a higher range than those paid for domestic travel. Even with respect to railways the European carriers pay commissions whereas no such commission on rail travel is paid in this country except in respect of the odd excursion, despite the fact that thousands of dollars are collected by the travel agents on behalf of the railways.
While there has been over the past few years a considerable increase in international travel there are still many thousands of our citizens who would prefer to spend their holidays in Canada. This is in some cases because these people have a "see Canada first" policy and in others because their means do not permit them to travel long distances, because their time is limited or because they prefer to spend their time at Canadian resorts. There are thousands who seek the advice of travel agents with respect to where they should spend their long week ends and there are many such places within easy reach which should be publicized and developed. No one
TMr. Beech.]
can do this better than the travel agent if he is given the proper information with which to work. I can only speak with respect to the province of Ontario because that is the only province of which I have any knowledge, but the department of travel and publicity in Ontario issues periodical information concerning motels, lodges and resorts in various parts of the province. This is particularly valuable because many people have no idea where they should spend their holidays and it is very handy to be able to go to a travel agent and get this information.
Complaints have been received that commercial fishermen have been allowed to deplete the stocks of fish in areas which might better have been designated tourist areas and a very good example of this is in the Georgian bay area where millions of dollars have been lost in the tourist business because of the loss of the lake trout fishing. Much of this has been lost because of the depredations of the lamprey, but I think a great deal of it can be attributed to the fact that the commercial fishermen were allowed to work in there, and they certainly depleted those stocks. Another complaint is that in certain provinces the liquor laws are too stringent.
The hon. member for Niagara Falls mentioned the operators who used the United States flag as a come-on. There is another type of operator who has a big sign advertising gasoline for 39 cents a gallon. Underneath, in very much smaller type, is added the fraction "nine-tenths" so as to be scarcely visible until you reach the point where you have to buy gasoline. In my opinion this is a sharp practice. It does not enhance the prestige of the Canadian businessman, and all these things do not encourage tourists to return to our country.
The best advertisement we can get is a satisfied tourist who goes back and tells his friends what a fine time he had in Canada. Tourism should be developed in such a way as to encourage a repeat business. Since everyone benefits as the tourist trade prospers, it is the business of everyone to foster that development, including the operator for whose benefit this resolution is designed. I congratulate the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) on having introduced this resolution, and on the manner in which he presented it, and I trust the government will give it favourable consideration. I shall conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, by saying that after the current session, hon. members from all parts of our country should start giving an example and visit Canada. Those from the west, for instance, could exchange visits with their representatives of central Canada and while giving leadership in this respect they would be able to know and to appreciate each other better.
I would encourage every hon. member of this house and all Canadians to visit my riding which is one of the richest from a geographic, economic and touristic point of view.
Indeed, you will find in my county the town of St. Lin, where our great autonomist, Sir Wilfrid Laurier was born, who would today sit in the ranks of the Conservative party if he were still living.
There is also the College of l'Assomption, where Sir Wilfrid Laurier was a pupil and, of course also the town of Joliette, on the banks of the Assomption river, which was founded by the Sieur Barthelemy de Joliette.
That is, Mr. Speaker, a very brief list of the touristic attractions in my riding.
There is also another place, the old manor of Mrs. McConville, where the late Lord Bennett spent a few days every year. These are resorts which deserve being known.
I therefore again urge all hon. members, as well as all Canadian citizens, to visit the riding of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm which is really a jewel from a tourist's point of view.
We should always keep in mind that the tourist industry is one of the most important industries of our country. Every citizen, whoever he may be, has the civic responsibility to try and make his small community, his home town, his own Canadian country, more attractive.
I therefore want to commend the hon. member who moved the resolution and I am asking the government, whether municipal, provincial or federal, to consider whether it would be opportune to subsidize that kind of private enterprise, so as to give to our municipalities, our provinces and our country as a whole, incomparable attraction which would draw large numbers of tourists to our country where they would spend the amount of dollars necessary to our economy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although the riding of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot, and not St. Hyacinthe Baghdad, as it has once been called in this house, is not
fMr. Pigeon.]

particularly known as a riding where the tourist industry is of prime importance, everyone would do well to visit it and specially the city of St. Hyacinthe which is rightly called St. Hyacinthe the fair one.
Mr. Speaker, even if this means repeating something that has already been said, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) for his fine contribution in submitting this resolution to the house. His speech was clear, concise and intelligent, as well as realistic. This resolution deserves the serious consideration of all members of the house. I therefore ask hon. members, no matter where they sit in this house, to give full consideration to his resolution.
Everyone is aware of the fact that the tourist industry brings us each year millions of dollars. A large number of small villages which, for the rest of the year, are barely known, become real cities during the tourist season owing to the large number of tourists coming in. It follows, of course, that trade expands considerably in such communities and that farmers as well as tradesmen take advantage of it. Everybody knows, without a doubt, that the province of Quebec offers exceptional attractions for tourists. There is the old Quebec inside Quebec city, which is of particular interest to the tourist. I may say that each year thousands of American tourists go there for a visit.
We have also, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Her-ridge) when he was speaking about his own riding, lakes by the thousands where fish is plentiful, where boating is practised on a large scale, and where the scenery is perhaps the main attraction for the tourists.
I therefore wish that this matter of tourist industry be seriously considered by the federal, provincial and municipal governments; I hope they will co-operate closely in order to develop this industry which brings us each year large sums of money.
It has become a common practice in the industry to grant workers and labourers longer and longer holidays, which allows them to put their spare time to good use, by improving their family's general knowledge through visits to these nationally important sites in their province or in the rest of the country.
It is therefore highly important to recognize the value of that industry, which is becoming one of the leading industries in this country, and to provide it with the assistance needed for its development.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I feel that
the resolution put forward by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken)

would contribute to the development of this country. So, while reiterating once more what I have just said, I would ask all hon. members to support the proposal, as I intend doing myself.
